questions.strategy: His words name the problem: sameness and lost independence. Pick the option that gives him some control back.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Sameness, loss of self-care and withdrawal from TV point to psychosocial effects of immobility.
Reassurance about traction skips his feelings.
Fewer visitors and sedation both increase withdrawal.

elimination.verdict: Give him choices in his own care.

questions.stem: A patient in intensive care with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome has an oxygen saturation of 86% while supine. The team turns her prone. Which finding indicates the positioning was effective?

options.text: Oxygen saturation rises to 93%
options.rationale: Prone positioning is first-line therapy for severe ARDS because it improves oxygenation. A rise from 86% shows it worked.

options.text: Skin over the sacrum stays intact
options.rationale: Prone takes pressure off the sacrum, so this is expected. It does not show that breathing improved.

options.text: She shows less restlessness in the bed
options.rationale: Comfort is a positioning goal, but restlessness can have many causes. The reason for prone here was oxygenation.

options.text: Heart rate stays at 96
options.rationale: An unchanged heart rate says nothing about gas exchange.

questions.takeaway: Match the outcome to the reason for the intervention. Prone positioning in severe ARDS is done to improve oxygenation.
questions.strategy: Ask why the team chose prone. The outcome that answers that question is the one that shows effectiveness.

steps.detail: Prone is first-line for severe ARDS to improve breathing.
Sacral skin and comfort are real positioning goals but not this one.
Saturation moved from 86% to 93%.

elimination.verdict: Oxygen saturation of 93%. The goal was oxygenation.

caseStudies.title: Fall with a suspected wrist fracture
caseStudies.intro: An 81 year old woman fell onto her outstretched right hand at her assisted living facility. She is in the emergency department with a splint on her right wrist while she waits for an x ray.

entries.text: Right wrist swollen with visible deformity. Splint applied by paramedics. Rates right wrist pain 7 out of 10. Right fingers pink and warm. Capillary refill 2 seconds. Radial pulse 2+ bilaterally. Reports new tingling in right thumb and index finger. Thoracic kyphosis noted. Moves slowly with a cane.
T 36.8 C; HR 96; RR 18; BP 148/84; SpO2 97% on room air

History of osteoporosis and osteoarthritis of both knees. Decreased range of motion in both shoulders. Lactose intolerant. Uses a cane for walking. Lives in assisted living and dresses herself. Right handed.
Calcium 8.6 mg/dL (9.0 to 10.5)
Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL (12 to 16)

question.nursesNote: 0900: Right wrist swollen with visible deformity. Rates right wrist pain 7 out of 10. Right fingers pink and warm. Capillary refill 2 seconds. Radial pulse 2+ bilaterally. Reports new tingling in right thumb and index finger. Thoracic kyphosis noted. Moves slowly with a cane.
question.stem: Which findings require immediate follow up? Highlight the findings.

segments.text: Right wrist swollen with visible deformity
segments.rationale: New deformity after a fall suggests a fracture.

segments.text: Rates right wrist pain 7 out of 10
segments.rationale: Severe pain needs follow up and a baseline to compare later.

segments.text: Right fingers pink and warm
segments.rationale: Normal color and temperature. Circulation is intact right now.

segments.text: Capillary refill 2 seconds
segments.rationale: Normal. Under 3 seconds.

segments.text: Radial pulse 2+ bilaterally
segments.rationale: Normal and equal on both sides.

segments.text: Reports new tingling in right thumb and index finger
segments.rationale: New numbness or tingling is a red flag. It can mean pressure on a nerve.

segments.text: Thoracic kyphosis noted
segments.rationale: An expected change with aging and osteoporosis. It is not new.

segments.text: Moves slowly with a cane
segments.rationale: Her baseline. Slowed movement is an expected change with aging.

question.takeaway: Separate what is new from what is her baseline. New deformity, severe pain and new tingling need follow up. Kyphosis and slow movement are expected with aging.
question.strategy: Kyphosis looks abnormal on a young adult. In an 81 year old with osteoporosis it is expected. Ask what is new today.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New deformity, severe pain and new tingling are on the deck list.

steps.action: Keep the normal circulation findings out
steps.detail: Pink, warm, 2 seconds and equal pulses are normal.
Kyphosis and a cane are her normal.

elimination.verdict: Swelling with deformity, pain 7 out of 10, new tingling.

question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected age related change or a finding that requires follow up.

rows.text: Thoracic kyphosis
rows.rationale: Bone loss with osteoporosis causes a humped upper back.

rows.text: Slowed movement
rows.rationale: Movement slows with aging. Do not rush her.

rows.text: Decreased range of motion in both shoulders
rows.rationale: ROM decreases with aging. It is equal on both sides.

rows.text: New tingling in the right thumb and index finger
rows.rationale: New and on the injured side only. This is a neurovascular change.

rows.text: Swelling and deformity of the right wrist
rows.rationale: New after a fall. A new deformity is a red flag.

rows.text: Serum calcium 8.6 mg/dL
rows.rationale: Below 9.0. Low calcium can reflect bone loss and is worth reporting.

question.takeaway: Aging changes are gradual and symmetric. Injury findings are new and one sided.
question.strategy: Low calcium is common in older adults, which makes it tempting to call it expected. A value outside the normal range still needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New findings after a fall need follow up.

steps.action: Ask whether it is on both sides
steps.detail: Symmetric loss is usually aging. One sided change is usually injury.

steps.action: Check the lab against its range
steps.detail: 8.6 is below 9.0.

elimination.verdict: Expected, expected, expected, follow up, follow up, follow up.

question.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
question.sentence: The nurse is most concerned that the client is at risk for [[1]] as evidenced by [[2]].

options.text: neurovascular compromise of the right hand
options.rationale: Swelling in a splinted, fractured wrist can press on nerves and vessels.

options.text: joint contracture of the right wrist
options.rationale: Contractures form over weeks of immobility. Not the concern today.

options.text: an osteoarthritis flare in the knees
options.rationale: Chronic and not related to today's injury.

options.text: pneumonia from immobility
options.rationale: She is not on bedrest and her SpO2 is 97% on room air.

options.text: new tingling in the right thumb and index finger
options.rationale: An early sign that a nerve is being compressed.

options.text: thoracic kyphosis
options.rationale: An expected aging change.

options.text: a heart rate of 96
options.rationale: Likely from pain and anxiety. It does not show the hand is at risk.

options.text: a history of lactose intolerance
options.rationale: A risk for low calcium over time. It says nothing about the hand today.

question.takeaway: After a fracture, the injured limb below the injury is the priority. Sensation changes are an early warning.
question.strategy: Lactose intolerance connects to her low calcium, which makes it feel important. It is a long term risk, not an acute threat.

steps.detail: A new fracture with swelling beats chronic problems.

steps.action: Find the finding that proves it
steps.detail: Tingling below the injury.
Contracture and lactose intolerance take weeks or years.

elimination.verdict: Neurovascular compromise; new tingling in the thumb and index finger.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse include in the neurovascular assessment of the right hand? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check color and temperature of the fingers
options.rationale: Pale or cool means poor blood flow.

options.text: Check capillary refill
options.rationale: A quick test of circulation to the fingertips.

options.text: Palpate the right radial pulse
options.rationale: The pulse shows blood flow to the hand. Grade it and compare with the left.

options.text: Assess sensation and movement of the fingers
options.rationale: Tests the nerves that pass the injury.

options.text: Compare each finding with the left hand
options.rationale: Always compare sides. The uninjured hand is her normal.

options.text: Ask her to move the right wrist through full range of motion
options.rationale: Moving a suspected fracture can cause more damage.

options.text: Use a Doppler first before trying to palpate pulses
options.rationale: The Doppler is used when a pulse cannot be felt. Palpate first.

question.takeaway: A neurovascular check covers color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement and pain, compared with the other side.
question.strategy: ROM is part of a musculoskeletal assessment. It is wrong on a limb with a suspected fracture.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement, pain.
Always compare with the other side.

steps.action: Reject what harms or skips a step
steps.detail: No ROM on a suspected fracture. Doppler only if pulses are not palpable.

elimination.verdict: Color and temperature, capillary refill, radial pulse, sensation and movement, compare sides.

entries.text: Right fingers pale and cool. Capillary refill 4 seconds. Right radial pulse weak. Numbness now in all right fingers. Rates pain 9 out of 10 despite prescribed analgesic. Swelling increased at edges of splint. Left hand pink and warm.

question.stem: Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Notify the provider of the neurovascular changes immediately
options.rationale: Pale, cool, weak pulse, spreading numbness and severe pain are all red flags to report now.

options.text: Recheck the hand in 1 hour
options.rationale: Waiting lets the damage continue.

options.text: Give another dose of the prescribed analgesic
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion is a warning sign. Treating the pain alone hides the problem.

options.text: Ask her to wiggle her fingers every 15 minutes
options.rationale: Movement helps assessment. It does not fix the circulation.

question.takeaway: Worsening neurovascular findings are an emergency. Report them to the provider immediately.
question.strategy: Pain relief is patient centered and sounds kind. Rising pain with pale cool fingers means circulation is failing.

steps.detail: Every neurovascular finding got worse.

steps.action: Match to the red flag list
steps.detail: Cool, pale, weak pulse, new numbness, severe pain, rapid swelling.

steps.action: Choose the action that fixes the cause
steps.detail: Only the provider can change the splint or treat the fracture.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider immediately.

entries.text: Provider loosened and reapplied splint. X ray confirms distal radius fracture. Right arm elevated on pillows.
Right fingers pink and warm. Capillary refill 2 seconds. Right radial pulse 2+ and equal to left. Rates pain 4 out of 10. Tingling remains in right thumb and index finger.

question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether the interventions were effective or not effective.

rows.text: Right fingers pink and warm
rows.rationale: Blood flow to the fingers is back.

rows.text: Capillary refill 2 seconds
rows.rationale: Back to normal from 4 seconds.

rows.text: Right radial pulse 2+ and equal to left
rows.rationale: The weak pulse is now strong and matches the other side.

rows.text: Pain rated 4 out of 10
rows.rationale: Down from 9 out of 10.

rows.text: Tingling remains in right thumb and index finger
rows.rationale: Present since 0900. The nerve findings still need monitoring and reporting.

question.takeaway: Circulation recovered after the splint was loosened. The tingling did not, so keep checking and report it.
question.strategy: Four findings improved, which invites you to call the whole picture better. The nerve finding did not change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Color, refill, pulse and pain all improved.

steps.action: Look for what did not change
steps.detail: Tingling has been there since 0900.
An unresolved finding stays on your list.

elimination.verdict: Effective, effective, effective, effective, not effective.

questions.stem: A daughter says her father forgets things that happened earlier in the day. Which response during the nurse's assessment supports her concern?

options.text: Counts backward from 100 by 7s without error
options.rationale: Serial 7s test attention. An accurate count shows attention is intact.

options.text: Explains that a stitch in time means fix problems early
options.rationale: Interpreting a saying tests abstract thinking. His answer is appropriate.

options.text: Cannot say how he got to the hospital this morning
options.rationale: Recalling a recent event tests recent memory. Failing it matches what the daughter sees.

options.text: Copies the word apple neatly onto paper
options.rationale: Copying tests a visual and motor task. It does not test memory.

questions.takeaway: Memory is tested by recall of a recent event. Serial 7s test attention. Sayings test abstract thinking.
questions.strategy: Name the function the concern points to. Find the response that shows that function failing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Forgetting recent events is a recent memory problem.
A tests attention. B tests abstract thinking. D tests a visual and motor task.
Only C shows he cannot recall a recent event.

elimination.verdict: C. The failed recall supports the daughter's concern.

questions.stem: An older adult patient who was oriented this morning suddenly becomes confused. What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: SpO2
options.rationale: Hypoxia is a fast, reversible cause of acute confusion and falls under breathing in the ABCs.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Infection can cause confusion, but oxygenation is the more immediate threat.

options.text: Medication reconciliation
options.rationale: Important later, but it takes time and does not address an immediate threat.

options.text: Electrolytes
options.rationale: Needs a lab draw and results; check oxygenation first.

questions.takeaway: A sudden change in mental status is a new cue that needs action now. Oxygenation is checked first because hypoxia is quick to find and quick to fix.
questions.strategy: When every option is a possible cause, use the ABCs to choose which one to check first.

steps.detail: Hypoxia, infection, medications, and electrolytes can all cause confusion.
Oxygenation is breathing, so it comes before the other causes.
SpO2 takes seconds at the bedside. Labs and a medication review take longer.

elimination.verdict: SpO2 is the priority because it is an ABC finding and the fastest to correct.

questions.stem: A patient with a frontal lobe injury has climbed out of bed twice despite being told to call for help. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Enable the bed alarm
options.rationale: Frontal lobe injury impairs judgment and impulse control. A bed alarm protects him without relying on his judgment.

options.text: Teach him again to use the call light before getting up
options.rationale: This depends on judgment and memory, the very functions the injury impairs. He has already ignored it twice.

options.text: Use a picture board for communication
options.rationale: Picture boards help aphasia. Nothing here suggests a language problem.

options.text: Place all items directly in front of him
options.rationale: This helps visual field loss or neglect, not impulsive behavior.

questions.takeaway: Frontal lobe damage impairs judgment and impulse control. Choose safety measures that do not depend on the patient deciding to follow them.
questions.strategy: Teaching sounds patient centered, but he cannot use it. Pick the measure that works without his judgment.

steps.action: Link the lobe to the behavior
steps.detail: Frontal lobe means poor judgment and impulsivity.
Repeating call light teaching has already failed.
Picture boards and item placement address other lobes.

elimination.verdict: Bed alarm.

questions.stem: A patient's Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15 at 0800. At 1200 the patient opens the eyes to voice, gives confused answers and obeys commands. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document an unchanged score and continue routine checks
options.rationale: Opening to voice and confusion both lower the score. It is no longer 15.

options.text: Prepare to protect the airway for a severely low score
options.rationale: The score is 13, not in the severe range. The patient still obeys commands.

options.text: Report the drop in score to the provider now
options.rationale: The new score is 13: eyes 3, verbal 4, motor 6. A declining score signals deterioration that needs immediate action.

options.text: Recheck the score at the next scheduled neuro check
options.rationale: Waiting delays action on a decline. The trend matters more than the single number.

questions.takeaway: Score E, V and M separately, then compare with the last score. Any decline calls for action now.
questions.strategy: Score the new findings before reading the options. Then compare the total with 15.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Opens to voice = 3.
Confused = 4. Obeys commands = 6.
3 + 4 + 6 = 13, a 2-point drop from 15.

elimination.verdict: C. A falling score is reported now.

questions.stem: A patient opens the eyes only to pain, moans without words and withdraws from a painful stimulus. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Complete a full cranial nerve assessment
options.rationale: Assessment continues once the airway is protected. ABCs come first.

options.text: Position the patient on the side with suction at the bedside
options.rationale: The score is 8: eyes 2, sounds 2, withdraws 4. A patient responding only to pain may not protect the airway.

options.text: Reorient the patient to person, place and time
options.rationale: The patient cannot respond in words. Reorienting does not address the danger.

options.text: Check the swallow with a sip of water
options.rationale: Fluid given to a patient who may not protect the airway risks aspiration.

questions.takeaway: Score the three parts, then read what the total means. A patient who responds only to pain may not guard the airway.
questions.strategy: Score the patient first. A very low score turns the question into an airway question.

steps.detail: Eyes to pain 2, moaning 2, withdrawal 4. Total 8.
Such a low score threatens the airway.
A delays airway care. C cannot work. D risks aspiration.

elimination.verdict: B. Protect the airway first.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients with head injuries. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Arms flexed tightly to the chest with wrists curled inward
options.rationale: This is decorticate posturing from damage above the brainstem. It is urgent but less severe than extension.

options.text: Arms stiffly extended at the sides with feet pointed down
options.rationale: Extension posturing is decerebrate. It signals brainstem involvement, the more severe of the two.

options.text: Reaches for the nurse's hand when the nail bed is pressed
options.rationale: Reaching toward a painful stimulus is localizing. It is purposeful.

options.text: Confused about the date, unchanged since admission
options.rationale: Stable confusion matches baseline. A new change would come first.

questions.takeaway: Both postures need immediate action. Extension points to the brainstem, so decerebrate outranks decorticate.
questions.strategy: Identify each posture from the arm position. Rank brainstem signs above signs from higher up.

steps.detail: C is purposeful. D is unchanged from baseline.
A is flexion toward the core. B is extension.
Extension means brainstem involvement, the worse sign.

elimination.verdict: B. Decerebrate posturing is seen first.

questions.stem: A patient has had slurred speech since a stroke last year. He names objects correctly and answers questions appropriately. Which communication approach should the nurse use?

options.text: Use a picture board because he cannot find words
options.rationale: He names objects correctly. Word finding is intact.

options.text: Give written instructions because he cannot understand speech
options.rationale: He answers appropriately. Understanding is intact.

options.text: Speak louder and more slowly to him
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a hearing problem. His difficulty is producing words, not receiving them.

options.text: Allow extra time and ask him to repeat unclear words
options.rationale: He chooses the right words but produces them poorly. That is a speech problem, so patience with repetition helps.

questions.takeaway: Language is understanding and choosing words. Speech is producing them. Match the approach to the part that failed.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the words are right. If they are right but sound wrong, support speech production.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He answers appropriately, so understanding is intact.
He names objects, so word finding is intact.
Slurring is a motor speech problem. Time and repetition help.

elimination.verdict: D. Support speech production.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old patient's daughter says, "Mom has been a little forgetful for years, but today she can't find her words and her right hand is weak. I guess it's just her age." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Slower thinking and some memory changes are expected at her age."
options.rationale: True of gradual changes, but it dismisses a sudden new deficit.

options.text: "These are sudden changes, so I'm going to assess her right now."
options.rationale: Sudden or new neurologic changes are never assumed to be aging. Assess immediately.

options.text: "Let's watch her for a few hours and see if it gets better."
options.rationale: Waiting delays care for a possible stroke.

options.text: "I'll ask the provider to order a memory test tomorrow."
options.rationale: Delays assessment of an acute change.

questions.takeaway: Aging slows processing, reflexes, and pupil response gradually. Sudden or one-sided changes are never aging and need immediate assessment.
questions.strategy: Separate gradual from sudden. The word "today" and a one-sided finding make this acute.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Word-finding trouble and right hand weakness started today.
A is technically true about aging but ignores the new deficit.
C and D postpone assessment.

elimination.verdict: B is correct because a new neurologic change means assess now.

questions.stem: The nurse is performing a cranial nerve assessment on a patient who is NPO for surgery. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Give a sip of water to test swallowing.
options.rationale: Never test swallowing with fluids when the patient is NPO.

options.text: Skip the swallow test and assess facial symmetry and pupils.
options.rationale: Swallowing is observed only if clinically appropriate. Other cranial nerve checks, including the gag reflex, still apply.

options.text: Give ice chips instead of water to test swallowing.
options.rationale: Ice chips are still something by mouth.

options.text: Postpone the entire neurologic assessment until after surgery.
options.rationale: Only the swallow part is deferred.

questions.takeaway: Do not test swallowing with fluids or ice chips if the patient is NPO. The gag reflex and the rest of the cranial nerves are still assessed as usual.
questions.strategy: Watch for options that quietly break an order, like ice chips for an NPO patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Give nothing by mouth when NPO. CN IX and X can still be checked with the gag reflex and uvula rise.
Ice chips still go by mouth.
D skips the whole assessment when only one part is off limits.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient admitted after a fall had pupils 3 mm, equal and brisk at 0800. Which finding at 1000 requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Both pupils 3 mm, round and brisk
options.rationale: This matches baseline.

options.text: Both pupils constrict to 2 mm under the penlight
options.rationale: Constricting to light is the expected reaction. 2 mm is within the normal range of 2 to 6 mm.

options.text: Right pupil 5 mm and sluggish, left 3 mm and brisk
options.rationale: The right pupil has grown and slowed since 0800. A new unequal, sluggish pupil can signal rising pressure on the brain.

options.text: Both pupils 4 mm and brisk in a dim room
options.rationale: Pupils widen slightly in dim light. They remain equal and brisk.

questions.takeaway: Record pupils in millimeters with equality and speed of reaction. A change from baseline matters most.
questions.strategy: Compare each option with the 0800 baseline. Look for a new inequality or a slowed reaction.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 3 mm, equal, brisk.
A matches baseline. B and D are normal reactions to light and dark.
Only C is unequal and sluggish.

elimination.verdict: C. A new unequal, sluggish pupil needs follow-up now.

questions.stem: A patient cannot feel a pinprick on the left foot but moves the foot strongly on command. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan?

options.text: Inspect the left foot daily for unnoticed injury
options.rationale: Sensation reaches the CNS on afferent pathways, which are impaired here. He will not feel an injury, so the nurse must look for it.

options.text: Assist with all walking because the leg is weak
options.rationale: Strong movement shows the efferent motor pathway works. Weakness is not the problem.

options.text: Perform passive range of motion on the left ankle
options.rationale: He moves the foot on his own. Passive motion is for patients who cannot.

options.text: Apply a heating pad to improve sensation
options.rationale: Heat on a numb foot risks a burn he cannot feel. It does not restore sensation.

questions.takeaway: Afferent pathways bring sensation in. Efferent pathways send movement out. When feeling is lost, the nurse becomes the warning system.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into sensory and motor. Plan for the part that failed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sensation is lost. Movement is intact.
Lost sensation is an afferent problem.
B and C treat movement, which works. D risks a burn.

elimination.verdict: A. Protect the foot he cannot feel.

questions.stem: A patient awaiting emergency surgery is terrified. His heart rate is 118 and his pupils are dilated. After the nurse coaches slow breathing, which finding indicates the intervention is effective?

options.text: Pupils remain dilated
options.rationale: Dilated pupils are a sympathetic sign. Unchanged pupils show no easing.

options.text: Heart rate falls to 86
options.rationale: Fear drives the sympathetic fight or flight response. A slower heart shows that response easing.

options.text: Respiratory rate rises to 26
options.rationale: Faster breathing points to more stress, not less.

options.text: States he still feels terrified
options.rationale: His fear is unchanged. The response driving his findings is still active.

questions.takeaway: Sympathetic means fight or flight: faster heart, dilated pupils. Calming should move each sign back toward rest and digest.
questions.strategy: Name the system driving the cues. The right answer shows that system settling.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fear, a fast heart and dilated pupils are sympathetic signs.
Only B moves a sign back toward rest.
A and D are unchanged. C is worse.

elimination.verdict: B. The slower heart rate shows the intervention worked.

questions.stem: After a witnessed episode of jerking in all four limbs followed by confusion, the provider orders a test to evaluate the event. Which patient statement shows understanding of the test?

options.text: It checks the nerves and muscles in my arms.
options.rationale: That describes EMG. The jerking started in the brain.

options.text: It records the electrical activity of my brain.
options.rationale: The episode suggests a seizure, which is abnormal brain electrical activity. An EEG records that activity.

options.text: They will take fluid from my lower back.
options.rationale: That is a lumbar puncture, which assesses CSF.

options.text: It measures the blood flow in my brain.
options.rationale: That is transcranial Doppler. Blood flow does not show seizure activity.

questions.takeaway: EEG shows brain electrical activity. EMG shows nerves and muscles. LP assesses CSF. Transcranial Doppler shows blood flow.
questions.strategy: Name the problem the event suggests. Then decide which test fits it before reading the statements.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Jerking of all limbs then confusion suggests a seizure.
A seizure is abnormal brain electrical activity, so the test is an EEG.
Only B describes an EEG.

elimination.verdict: B. The patient understands the EEG.

questions.stem: A patient admitted for pneumonia had a normal neurologic exam on admission. Today the nurse notices a new tremor in the left hand. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Repeat the complete head-to-toe neurologic exam
options.rationale: A comprehensive exam sets a broad baseline for new admissions. A baseline already exists.

options.text: Perform a focused neurologic assessment and compare with baseline
options.rationale: A change from baseline calls for a focused assessment. It targets the new finding quickly.

options.text: Document the tremor and recheck at the next shift
options.rationale: A new neurologic finding needs assessment now.

options.text: Notify the provider before assessing further
options.rationale: The nurse assesses first so the report carries data.

questions.takeaway: Comprehensive sets a broad baseline for new admissions. Focused targets a change from baseline or a known problem.
questions.strategy: Ask what triggered the assessment: a new admission or a new change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A new finding against an established baseline.
A change from baseline calls for a focused assessment.
C waits. D calls without data.

elimination.verdict: B. Focused assessment now.

questions.stem: A patient says her face feels "crooked," and the nurse notices new drooling from the left corner of her mouth. Which assessment does the nurse perform next?

options.text: Ask her to follow a finger with her eyes.
options.rationale: Eye movements test CN III, IV and VI. They do not address the facial finding.

options.text: Ask her to smile, raise her eyebrows and show her teeth.
options.rationale: These test CN VII, which moves the face. The nurse compares both sides for droop.

options.text: Ask her to swallow a sip of water.
options.rationale: Swallowing (CN IX and X) is tested only if appropriate. Drooling suggests she may not swallow safely.

options.text: Ask her to shrug her shoulders.
options.rationale: Shoulder shrug tests CN XI.

questions.takeaway: CN VII: smile, raise eyebrows, show teeth and compare both sides. CN IX and X: observe swallowing only if appropriate.
questions.strategy: Match the finding to the nerve that moves that part. Then check that the test is safe for this patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A crooked face and drooling point to the facial nerve, CN VII.
Eyes are III, IV and VI. Shrug is XI.
Water before a safe swallow is confirmed risks aspiration.

elimination.verdict: B is the next assessment.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old patient who was alert and oriented this morning is suddenly confused. Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check the oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Hypoxia is a fast, reversible cause. It is also the quickest to check.

options.text: Check a fingerstick blood glucose
options.rationale: Low or high glucose commonly causes acute confusion.

options.text: Check the temperature
options.rationale: Infection, including UTI or sepsis, often presents as confusion in older adults.

options.text: Review medications given since this morning
options.rationale: Sedatives, opioids and anticholinergics are common causes.

options.text: Review the most recent sodium level
options.rationale: Sodium imbalance in particular affects the brain.

options.text: Document the change as expected for age
options.rationale: Aging is gradual. A sudden change is never assumed to be aging.

options.text: Reorient the patient and recheck in 4 hours
options.rationale: Waiting delays finding the cause. A sudden change needs assessment now.

questions.takeaway: For a sudden mental status change, check oxygenation, glucose, infection, medications and electrolytes. Never blame aging.
questions.strategy: Keep every action that looks for an acute cause now. Remove any option that explains away or delays.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Alert this morning, confused now, is a sudden change.
Oxygen, glucose, temperature, medications and sodium.
F blames age. G waits.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D and E.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses an 82-year-old patient. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Slower reaction time
options.rationale: Processing speed and reaction time slow with age.

options.text: Diminished deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Expected with aging.

options.text: New weakness of the left arm
options.rationale: One-sided weakness is not aging. Assess immediately.

options.text: Decreased sensitivity to touch and temperature
options.rationale: Expected. It is a burn and injury risk to teach about.

questions.takeaway: Aging slows things down evenly and gradually. New, sudden, or one-sided changes are not aging.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by speed of onset and symmetry.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reaction time, reflexes and sensation are expected with aging.
New arm weakness needs action.

elimination.verdict: C. New one-sided weakness is never aging.

questions.scenario:
82-year-old man, admitted 2 days ago.
Baseline: alert, oriented x 4, face symmetric.
Pupils 3 mm, equal, brisk.
questions.stem: The nurse assesses this patient on the morning of day 3. For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected age-related change or requires follow-up.

rows.text: Pauses before answering but answers correctly
rows.rationale: Slower processing with correct answers is expected with aging.

rows.text: Right corner of the mouth droops when smiling
rows.rationale: His face was symmetric at baseline. New facial asymmetry suggests a stroke.

rows.text: Woke twice overnight but fell back asleep easily
rows.rationale: More nighttime waking is an expected sleep change.

rows.text: Left pupil 6 mm and sluggish, right pupil 3 mm and brisk
rows.rationale: Baseline was 3 mm and equal. New inequality with a sluggish reaction can signal rising pressure.

rows.text: Ankle reflexes diminished on both sides
rows.rationale: Diminished deep tendon reflexes on both sides are expected.

rows.text: Calls the nurse by his daughter's name
rows.rationale: He was oriented x 4 at baseline. New confusion is never assumed to be aging.

questions.takeaway: Expected aging changes are gradual and symmetric. A finding that differs from this patient's baseline needs follow-up.
questions.strategy: Check each row against the baseline in the excerpt. Anything new, sudden or one-sided needs follow-up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rows 2, 4 and 6 contradict the documented face, pupils and orientation.
Rows 1, 3 and 5 are slowing, sleep and reflex changes expected with age.

elimination.verdict: Expected: 1, 3, 5. Follow-up: 2, 4, 6.

questions.stem: A patient who was alert and oriented 30 minutes ago now has new confusion, slurred speech and right-sided weakness. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the stroke alert
options.rationale: Escalation is needed, but it is the last step of the class sequence so the call carries the data the team needs.

options.text: Reorient the patient and recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Waiting treats a sudden change as minor. A new neurologic change is never watched and rechecked later.

options.text: Compare the findings with the prior baseline
options.rationale: You need current findings before you have anything to compare.

options.text: Assess the patient immediately at the bedside
options.rationale: A new neurologic change means act now, and acting starts with assessing the patient in front of you.

questions.takeaway: A new neurologic change means act now: recognize, assess, compare, ABCs and vital signs, then notify. On the NCLEX, if the patient looks unstable, the ABCs come first.
questions.strategy: Calling for help feels like the fastest response. The call is useful only once you have assessed.

steps.detail: Alert 30 minutes ago, now confused and weak on one side.
Reorienting and rechecking delays care.
Assess, then compare, then notify.

elimination.verdict: Assess the patient immediately.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews Glasgow Coma Scale scores for four patients on a neurology unit. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: GCS 9, unchanged over the past 8 hours
options.rationale: The score is low but stable. It is not the patient who is getting worse.

options.text: GCS 12, down from 14 an hour ago
options.rationale: A falling score signals deterioration and needs action now.

options.text: GCS 15, unchanged since admission
options.rationale: Fully alert and stable.

options.text: GCS 10, up from 8 this morning
options.rationale: The trend shows improvement.

questions.takeaway: GCS scores eyes (1 to 4), verbal (1 to 5) and motor (1 to 6) for a range of 3 to 15. The trend matters more than one number. A falling score means act now.
questions.strategy: Look at the direction of each score, not its size. Declining beats low but stable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A is stable. C is stable. D is improving.
Only B is falling.
The lowest number, 9, is stable and does not come first.

elimination.verdict: B. The declining patient is seen first.

questions.stem: A patient was alert and oriented at 0800. At 1100 the nurse assesses him again. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Hand grips equal and strong
options.rationale: A stable motor finding. Nothing has declined.

options.text: Opens eyes only when his name is called loudly
options.rationale: He was alert at 0800. A drop in level of consciousness is the earliest sign of neurologic decline.

options.text: Reports mild hunger
options.rationale: Not a neurologic finding.

options.text: Pupils 3 mm, equal and brisk, as at 0800
options.rationale: Unchanged from baseline.

questions.takeaway: Compare every finding to baseline. A decline in level of consciousness means assess and report now.
questions.strategy: Three options are stable or unrelated. One is a change from the 0800 baseline.

steps.detail: Alert and oriented at 0800.
Equal grips and unchanged pupils.
Hunger is not neurologic.

elimination.verdict: Eyes open only to a loud voice.

questions.stem: A patient's Glasgow Coma Scale score was 14 at 0800 and is 11 at 1000. Which statement by the new graduate caring for him indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "A drop of 3 points means he is getting worse, so I will act now."
options.rationale: Correct. A declining score signals deterioration.

options.text: "I score his eye, verbal and motor responses separately, then add them."
options.rationale: Correct. These are the three GCS components.

options.text: "His score of 11 is mid range, so I will recheck at the usual time."
options.rationale: This reads one number and ignores the trend. The fall from 14 needs action now.

options.text: "Even at his worst, the lowest score he could get is 3."
options.rationale: Correct. Each component scores at least 1.

questions.takeaway: One GCS score is a snapshot. The trend shows whether the patient is getting better or worse.
questions.strategy: In a further teaching item, find the one false statement. Here it is the one that ignores the drop from 14 to 11.

steps.detail: Look for the statement that is wrong.
A, B and D match the slide.
C treats 11 as a stand alone number and delays action.

elimination.verdict: C requires further teaching.

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury flexed his arms tightly to his chest when given a trapezius squeeze yesterday. Today the same stimulus makes his arms and legs extend rigidly. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the change to the provider now as a neurologic decline
options.rationale: Flexion to the core is decorticate posturing, motor 3. Rigid extension is decerebrate, motor 2, and means the brainstem is now involved.

options.text: Document an improvement in his motor response
options.rationale: The direction is reversed. Moving from flexion to extension is a decline.

options.text: Document withdrawal from pain, a normal response
options.rationale: Withdrawal moves away from the stimulus. Posturing looks the same wherever the pain is applied.

options.text: Continue routine checks since the motor score is unchanged
options.rationale: The score dropped from 3 to 2. Any decline needs action now.

questions.takeaway: Decorticate is flexion to the core, motor 3. Decerebrate is extension, motor 2, brainstem and worse. A change from one to the other is a decline you report.
questions.strategy: Two options call the change good or neutral. Decide the direction first, then the action follows.

steps.detail: Flexion yesterday, extension today.
Extension scores lower and means brainstem involvement.
Report now.

elimination.verdict: Report the decline now.

questions.scenario: A 71-year-old taking warfarin was admitted after a fall at home. At 1600 he was alert and oriented x4, GCS 15, pupils 3 mm, equal and brisk. At 1900 he opens his eyes when his name is spoken, says he is "at the store" and squeezes and releases the nurse's hand on command. The right pupil is now 4 mm and sluggish. His wife says, "He is always tired by evening."
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Check airway, breathing and vital signs at the bedside
options.rationale: A falling LOC can compromise the airway. You confirm ABCs before anything else.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately using the 1600 findings as the comparison
options.rationale: The slides say a declining score requires immediate action. Giving the baseline makes the change clear.

options.text: Let him sleep and repeat the GCS at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: The correct step at the wrong time. Waiting until the next scheduled check on a patient taking warfarin with a new pupil change can cost brain tissue.

options.text: Reorient him and dim the lights for evening confusion
options.rationale: Accepts the wife's explanation. He was oriented three hours ago, so this is a new change, not a pattern.

options.text: Declining level of consciousness indicating neurologic deterioration
options.rationale: GCS fell from 15 to 13 (E3 V4 M6) and one pupil became larger and sluggish. Both are changes from his own baseline.

options.text: Normal evening fatigue
options.rationale: Fatigue does not make a person disoriented or change one pupil.

options.text: Stable status because the GCS is still above 8
options.rationale: True that 13 is not a coma score. The trend is what matters. A drop of 2 in three hours is significant.

options.text: Decerebrate posturing
options.rationale: He obeys commands, which scores motor 6. Posturing would score 2 or 3.

options.text: GCS with each component recorded
options.rationale: Recording E, V and M shows exactly which response is changing and lets everyone compare the same way.

options.text: Pupil size in millimeters and reaction to light
options.rationale: An oval or sluggish pupil that is growing is an early warning of pressure on CN III. Millimeters let you compare with the last check.

options.text: Orientation to time only
options.rationale: Too narrow. It misses eye opening, motor response and pupils.

options.text: Temperature every 4 hours
options.rationale: Useful in general care, but it does not track the problem he has now.

questions.takeaway: A drop in GCS from the patient's own baseline is a new cue that needs action now, even when the number still looks acceptable.
questions.strategy: The wife's comment and a GCS still above 8 invite you to wait. A change in level of consciousness comes first, and vital sign changes come late.

steps.detail: Eyes to voice 3, confused 4, obeys 6. Total 13, down from 15.
New disorientation and a new unequal, sluggish pupil.

steps.action: Reject the explanations that delay care
steps.detail: Evening fatigue and a score above 8 do not explain a change.
ABCs, notify, then GCS components and pupils.

elimination.verdict: Neurologic deterioration; check ABCs and notify now; track GCS components and pupils in mm.

questions.stem: An alert patient reports new numbness in the left hand. The nurse observes a student assessing sensation. Which action by the student requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Asks the patient to close both eyes before testing
options.rationale: Closed eyes keep vision from guiding the answers. This is correct technique.

options.text: Asks whether the touch feels the same on both sides
options.rationale: This is the side comparison the assessment requires.

options.text: Uses light touch rather than nail bed pressure
options.rationale: The patient is alert. A painful stimulus is reserved for decreased LOC.

options.text: Tests light touch on the left hand only
options.rationale: Sensation is always compared right and left. Without the right hand there is no control.

questions.takeaway: Sensory checks are comparisons. Test both sides with the eyes closed. Match the stimulus to the LOC.
questions.strategy: The question asks for the wrong action. Treat each option as correct or incorrect technique.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Look for the action that is wrong.
Testing only the left hand removes the control side.
Closed eyes, side comparison and light touch in an alert patient are all correct.

elimination.verdict: D. The student must test both hands.

questions.stem: Patient 1 slurs but uses correct words. Patient 2 speaks fluent sentences that make no sense. Patient 3 has a new facial droop and is due for oral medications. Which action is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Document patient 1's change as a speech problem
options.rationale: Accurate, since the words are right and producing them is the problem. It is documentation, not the priority.

options.text: Hold patient 3's pills, keep her NPO and notify the provider
options.rationale: Facial weakness can come with weak swallowing muscles. A new droop is also an acute change the provider needs now.

options.text: Call the rapid response team for patient 2
options.rationale: Possibly urgent, but first make sure a hearing or language barrier is not causing the finding.

options.text: Check patient 2's hearing and primary language
options.rationale: A good step that takes seconds. No airway is at risk.

questions.takeaway: Slurred with the right words is speech. Wrong words is language. Protect the airway and report a new facial droop before giving pills.
questions.strategy: Several options are correct actions. Only one protects an airway.

steps.detail: Patient 1 speech, patient 2 language, patient 3 a new droop.
Patient 3 is about to swallow pills.
Documentation and hearing checks can wait.

elimination.verdict: Hold patient 3's pills and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old admitted after a fall opens her eyes to a loud voice and speaks random words. Asked to squeeze the nurse's fingers, she grips both hands firmly. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Score the motor response as obeys commands
options.rationale: A grasp can be a reflex. A strong grip does not prove she understood the words.

options.text: Apply nail bed pressure to see whether she localizes pain
options.rationale: She responds to voice, so a painful stimulus is not needed yet. Least noxious first.

options.text: Document the grips as normal and check her pupils
options.rationale: The motor score is still unproven.

options.text: Ask her to let go and hold up two fingers, then score
options.rationale: Releasing on command and a second simple task cannot happen by reflex. That proves command following.

questions.takeaway: A strong grip is not command following. Ask the patient to let go or do a second simple task before you score obeys.
questions.strategy: A firm grip looks like success. Ask what a reflex could also produce.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Grasping can be reflexive.
She responds to voice.
Letting go on command proves understanding.

elimination.verdict: Ask her to let go and hold up two fingers.

questions.nursesNote: 1200: 81-year-old admitted at 0700 after striking her head in a fall at home. Takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Right pupil 3 mm and slightly oval since cataract surgery, unchanged from 0800. Left pupil now 5 mm and sluggish, was 3 mm and brisk at 0800. Diminished ankle reflexes bilaterally. Decreased vibration sense in both feet. Oriented to person and place only, was oriented x4 at 0800. Right hand grip now weaker than left, equal at 0800. Slow to rise from the chair and walks with a cane as at home. Reports a headache that is getting worse.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

segments.text: Right pupil 3 mm and slightly oval since cataract surgery, unchanged from 0800
segments.rationale: Oval since surgery and unchanged. A known baseline irregularity is not a new finding.

segments.text: Left pupil now 5 mm and sluggish, was 3 mm and brisk at 0800
segments.rationale: A new size increase with a slower reaction on one side is an early warning of CN III compression.

segments.text: Diminished ankle reflexes bilaterally
segments.rationale: Expected with aging and symmetric.

segments.text: Decreased vibration sense in both feet
segments.rationale: Expected with aging when it is bilateral and gradual.

segments.text: Oriented to person and place only, was oriented x4 at 0800
segments.rationale: A drop in orientation over four hours is a change from baseline. LOC and orientation change first.

segments.text: Right hand grip now weaker than left, equal at 0800
segments.rationale: New one-sided weakness is focal. It points to the opposite hemisphere.

segments.text: Slow to rise from the chair and walks with a cane as at home
segments.rationale: Her baseline mobility. Slower movement is an expected age change.

segments.text: Reports a headache that is getting worse
segments.rationale: A worsening headache after a head strike can mean a growing bleed and rising ICP.

questions.takeaway: Compare each finding to her own baseline. Gradual symmetric changes are aging. New, one-sided, or worsening changes need action now.
questions.strategy: The oval pupil is the trap. It is abnormal but documented at baseline. Ask of every finding whether it is new since 0800.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A head strike on warfarin raises the chance of a bleed.
Oval right pupil, cane use, reflexes and vibration sense are baseline or aging.
Left pupil, orientation, right grip and headache all changed since 0800.

elimination.verdict: Left pupil change, lost orientation, new right grip weakness and worsening headache.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old who was alert and oriented this morning is suddenly confused with an SpO2 of 86%. The nurse applies oxygen per protocol. Which finding 30 minutes later indicates the intervention was effective?

options.text: SpO2 96%, sleeping and difficult to arouse
options.rationale: Oxygenation improved but LOC has declined. Being hard to arouse needs immediate follow up.

options.text: SpO2 94%, awake but says the year is 1998
options.rationale: He is still disoriented. Mental status has not returned to baseline.

options.text: SpO2 95%, alert and oriented to person, place, time and situation
options.rationale: Oxygenation improved and he is back to his morning baseline.

options.text: SpO2 92%, picking at the IV line
options.rationale: Oxygenation is still low. Picking at lines suggests ongoing confusion.

questions.takeaway: A sudden change in mental status is a new cue. Oxygenation is one of the first causes to check. The intervention worked only when the patient returns to baseline.
questions.strategy: Look for the option where both the SpO2 and the mental status are back to baseline.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A, B and C show better oxygenation. D is still low.
A shows lower LOC. B shows ongoing disorientation.
Only C matches the morning baseline.

elimination.verdict: C shows the intervention was effective.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches the daughter of an 82-year-old patient about expected neurologic changes with aging. Which statement by the daughter indicates the teaching was understood?

options.text: "Sudden forgetfulness is just her age, so I don't need to call."
options.rationale: Sudden changes always need immediate assessment. They are never blamed on aging.

options.text: "Sudden confusion or weakness on one side means I get help right away."
options.rationale: She recognizes that sudden neurologic changes are not due to aging.

options.text: "Her slower reaction time means her brain is failing."
options.rationale: Slower processing and reaction time are expected with aging.

options.text: "Waking up at night means something is wrong with her brain."
options.rationale: More nighttime waking is an expected change with aging.

questions.takeaway: Slower movements, slower processing, diminished reflexes and more nighttime waking are expected with aging. Sudden neurologic changes are never assumed to be aging.
questions.strategy: Separate expected gradual changes from sudden ones. The correct statement treats sudden change as urgent.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A and B both describe a sudden change. A dismisses it and B acts on it.
C and D describe normal aging but label it as disease.

elimination.verdict: B shows the teaching was understood.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old has reduced sensation to temperature in both feet, which is unchanged from baseline. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care?

options.text: Check bath water temperature with a thermometer before use
options.rationale: Correct. She cannot feel water that is too hot. The nurse protects her from burns.

options.text: Apply a heating pad to warm her feet at night
options.rationale: Heat she cannot feel can burn her. This adds risk.

options.text: Notify the provider of a new sensory deficit
options.rationale: Unchanged from baseline and expected with aging. No new change to report.

options.text: Keep her in bed to prevent injury
options.rationale: Immobility creates new problems. The risk is burns, not walking.

questions.takeaway: Decreased temperature sensation is an expected aging change. The nursing job is to protect against burns.
questions.strategy: Baseline tells you whether to report or to plan. Unchanged means you plan for safety.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Unchanged, so it is expected aging.
She cannot sense heat, so burns are the danger.
Measure the water. Avoid heat devices.

elimination.verdict: Check water temperature with a thermometer.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old with diabetes becomes suddenly confused. Blood glucose is 52 mg/dL. The nurse gives oral glucose per protocol. Which finding 15 minutes later indicates the intervention was effective?

options.text: Oriented to person, place, time and situation with glucose 104 mg/dL
options.rationale: Correct. Both the cause and the symptom have resolved.

options.text: She drank the full 4 ounces of juice
options.rationale: Taking the treatment is not the same as responding to it.

options.text: She is resting quietly with her eyes closed
options.rationale: Could be improvement or a falling LOC. You must arouse her to know.

options.text: Pupils 3 mm, equal and briskly reactive
options.rationale: Normal, but pupils were not the problem. They do not show that the confusion cleared.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate with the same cue that triggered the action. Here that is orientation and the glucose value.
questions.strategy: Sudden confusion has an acute cause. Recheck the cause and the mental status together.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden confusion with low glucose.
Orientation returns and glucose is normal.

steps.action: Cut the process and unrelated findings
steps.detail: Drinking juice is a process. Pupils were never abnormal.

elimination.verdict: Oriented with a normal glucose. The acute cause is corrected.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with multiple sclerosis is admitted during a flare. Which statement by the patient requires follow up?

options.text: "I stopped seeing my friends. Nothing feels worth doing anymore."
options.rationale: Correct. Withdrawal and hopelessness are depression cues. Chronic neurologic conditions raise that risk, so screen now.

options.text: "I get very tired by late afternoon."
options.rationale: Fatigue is common with this condition. Plan rest, but it is not the priority.

options.text: "My church group brings us meals every week."
options.rationale: A support system is a strength. Nothing to act on.

options.text: "I use a cane when I walk long distances."
options.rationale: A safe adaptation to her mobility limits.

questions.takeaway: A neuro assessment includes psychosocial status. Screen for depression in chronic neurologic illness.
questions.strategy: Three statements describe coping or expected symptoms. One describes a mood change that could become a safety issue.

steps.detail: Fatigue is expected. Church and cane are strengths.
Withdrawal and hopelessness suggest depression.
Depression screening is part of the neuro assessment.

elimination.verdict: The withdrawal statement. It needs a depression screen.

caseStudies.title: Serial neuro checks after a fall
caseStudies.intro: A 67 year old man was admitted overnight for observation after he fell at home and struck the right side of his head. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation.

entries.text: Fell in his kitchen at 0200 and hit the right side of his head on the counter. No loss of consciousness per wife.
History: atrial fibrillation on warfarin; hypertension; cataract surgery in both eyes 2 years ago.
Head CT on arrival: no bleeding. Admitted for neuro checks every 2 hours.
Baseline per wife: sharp, independent, speaks clearly, reads the paper daily.
Alert and oriented x4. Speech clear. GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6). Pupils 3 mm, equal, round, brisk. Hand grips strong and equal. Bruise on right forehead. Denies headache.

Oriented to person and place, not to time. Restless, keeps pulling at the blanket. Reports headache 6 of 10, new since 0800. Opens eyes spontaneously. Follows commands. Right pupil 4 mm and sluggish; left pupil 3 mm and brisk. Left hand grip weaker than right.
T 36.8 C; HR 82 irregular; RR 16; BP 138/82; SpO2 97% on room air
T 36.9 C; HR 80 irregular; RR 16; BP 146/80; SpO2 96% on room air
INR 3.6 (goal 2 to 3 on warfarin)
Glucose 104 mg/dL (70 to 110)
Sodium 139 mEq/L (135 to 145)

question.nursesNote: 1000: Neuro check due. Oriented to person and place, not to time. Restless, keeps pulling at the blanket. Reports headache 6 of 10, new since 0800. Right pupil 4 mm and sluggish; left pupil 3 mm and brisk. Left hand grip weaker than right. Bruise on right forehead, unchanged from admission. Reading glasses at bedside. Skin warm and dry.
question.stem: Which findings require immediate follow up? Highlight the findings.

segments.text: Oriented to person and place, not to time
segments.rationale: He was oriented x4 at 0800. New disorientation is a drop in mental status, the earliest sign of neurologic decline.

segments.text: Restless, keeps pulling at the blanket
segments.rationale: Restlessness is an early sign of rising pressure in the skull. In a man who was calm 2 hours ago it is not simple anxiety.

segments.text: Reports headache 6 of 10, new since 0800
segments.rationale: A new headache after a head injury in a client on warfarin points to a possible bleed.

segments.text: Right pupil 4 mm and sluggish; left pupil 3 mm and brisk
segments.rationale: Pupils were equal and brisk at 0800. A new unequal, sluggish pupil is an early warning of pressure on the third cranial nerve.

segments.text: Left hand grip weaker than right
segments.rationale: New asymmetry. The right side of the brain controls the left hand. He struck the right side of his head.

segments.text: Bruise on right forehead, unchanged from admission
segments.rationale: Present at admission and unchanged. It explains the fall, not the new decline.

segments.text: Reading glasses at bedside
segments.rationale: Irrelevant to his neurologic status.

segments.text: Skin warm and dry
segments.rationale: Normal finding.

question.takeaway: Compare every neuro check with the last one. New confusion, restlessness, headache, a sluggish pupil or new weakness on one side all need action now.
question.strategy: The bruise is abnormal and it is a trap. It was there at 0800, so it is not a change from baseline.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every finding at 1000 is judged against it.
Orientation, restlessness, headache, pupil and grip all changed.
The bruise, glasses and skin are baseline or normal.

elimination.verdict: Disorientation, restlessness, new headache, the unequal pupil and the weak left grip.

question.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
question.sentence:
At 0800 the client's Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15. At 1000 his score is [[1]].

Compared with 0800, this change [[2]].

The earliest sign of neurologic decline in this client was [[3]].

options.rationale: Eyes open spontaneously (4), confused verbal response (4), obeys commands (6). 4 plus 4 plus 6 is 14.
This would require eye opening only to voice. He opens his eyes spontaneously.
He is no longer oriented, so verbal is 4, not 5.
Motor is still 6 because he follows commands.

options.text: is a decline from baseline that needs action now
options.rationale: The trend matters more than a single number. Any drop in a client who was 15 is new information to act on.

options.text: is within normal limits because 14 is close to 15
options.rationale: Close to normal is not the question. Different from his own baseline is.

options.text: is expected with aging in a 67 year old
options.rationale: Aging is gradual. A change over 2 hours is never aging.

options.text: can wait for the next scheduled check at 1200
options.rationale: Waiting lets a bleed keep growing inside a skull that cannot expand.

options.text: the change in orientation and restlessness
options.rationale: Level of consciousness changes first because the cerebral cortex is the most sensitive to low blood flow and oxygen.

options.text: the unequal pupils
options.rationale: An important finding that usually follows the change in mental status.

options.text: the change in blood pressure
options.rationale: Vital sign changes come late, when the brainstem is compressed.

options.text: the bruise on his forehead
options.rationale: Present on admission. It is the reason for concern, not a sign of decline.

question.takeaway: Score the best response in each part of the GCS. The trend over time is what signals deterioration.
question.strategy: In the first blank, only the verbal score changed. Confused is 4. Following commands is motor 6, not verbal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 15 to 14 is a drop, however small.
Mental status first, pupils next, vital signs last.

elimination.verdict: 14; a decline that needs action now; the change in orientation and restlessness.

question.stem: Which explanation for the client's findings is most likely?

options.text: Rising pressure inside the skull from bleeding in the brain
options.rationale: A head injury, warfarin with an INR of 3.6 and a new decline on one side all fit a bleed that is slowly raising pressure.

options.text: Normal age related slowing of thinking and reflexes
options.rationale: Aging is gradual. This happened in 2 hours. Never label a sudden change as aging.

options.text: Low blood glucose causing confusion
options.rationale: Low glucose mimics a neuro change, so recheck it with a fingerstick. His 0600 glucose was 104. Low glucose also does not explain an unequal pupil or weakness on one side.

options.text: Anxiety from being in an unfamiliar hospital room
options.rationale: Anxiety does not cause an unequal pupil or a weak hand on one side.

question.takeaway: Before you call a change anxiety or aging, rule out the dangerous cause the chart already points to.
question.strategy: Link the history to the findings. The fall, the warfarin and the high INR explain the new pupil and grip changes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose is normal.
Aging and anxiety do not cause signs on one side.
Head injury on a blood thinner with a high INR.

elimination.verdict: Rising pressure inside the skull from a bleed.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse plan now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess airway, breathing and SpO2
options.rationale: ABCs come first in any acute neuro change.

options.text: Compare all findings with the 0800 neuro check
options.rationale: The slide sequence: recognize, assess, compare with baseline, check ABCs and vital signs, then notify.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately using SBAR
options.rationale: A new neuro change needs the provider now, not at rounds.

options.text: Increase neuro checks to more often than every 2 hours
options.rationale: A declining client needs closer monitoring to catch the next change.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed raised about 30 degrees with the head midline
options.rationale: Helps venous blood drain from the skull.

options.text: Document the restlessness as anxiety and offer a sedative
options.rationale: Sedation masks the level of consciousness, the finding you most need to watch.

options.text: Recheck at the scheduled 1200 neuro check to confirm the trend
options.rationale: The trend is already clear. Waiting 2 hours delays care for a possible bleed.

question.takeaway: A new neuro change means act now: ABCs, compare with baseline, notify, then watch more closely.
question.strategy: Look for options that delay or hide the change. Sedating and waiting both do.

steps.detail: ABCs first.
Compare with baseline, then notify.

steps.action: Cut anything that hides or delays
steps.detail: Sedation and waiting.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

entries.text: Provider notified by SBAR. Stat head CT ordered. Transport pending.
Opens eyes only to loud voice. Says random words. Withdraws from nail bed pressure. GCS 10 (E3 V3 M4). Right pupil 5 mm, sluggish. Airway clear; SpO2 95%.

question.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Stay with the client and activate the rapid response team
options.rationale: His GCS fell 4 points in 40 minutes. That is rapid deterioration. He needs help at the bedside now.

options.text: Give the scheduled oral warfarin dose with sips of water
options.rationale: He may be bleeding and his level of consciousness is falling. Oral intake also risks aspiration.

options.text: Reorient the client to time and place and document the confusion
options.rationale: Reorienting treats nothing. The problem is his brain, not his knowledge of the date.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat to improve blood flow to the brain
options.rationale: Lying flat slows venous drainage and can raise pressure in the skull.

question.takeaway: A falling GCS is an emergency. Stay with the client and bring help to the bedside.
question.strategy: The oral dose looks routine. With a falling level of consciousness, nothing goes by mouth.

steps.detail: E3 V3 M4 is 10, down from 14.
Oral warfarin and lying flat both add risk.

steps.action: Pick the action that matches the speed
steps.detail: Rapid decline needs the rapid response team.

elimination.verdict: Stay with him and activate the rapid response team.

entries.text: CT: small bleed over the right side of the brain. Warfarin reversed as prescribed. Neuro checks every hour.

Opens eyes to normal voice. Confused about place and time. Follows the command to squeeze both hands. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Right pupil 4 mm and brisk; left pupil 3 mm and brisk. Left hand grip remains weaker than right. Left corner of the mouth droops when he smiles. BP 136/80; HR 78 irregular.

question.stem: For each 1400 finding, indicate whether it has improved or has not improved compared with 1040.

rows.text: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
rows.rationale: Up from 10. The verbal and motor scores both rose.

rows.text: Follows the command to squeeze both hands
rows.rationale: At 1040 he only withdrew from pain. Obeying commands is motor 6.

rows.text: Right pupil 4 mm and brisk
rows.rationale: Smaller and brisk, compared with 5 mm and sluggish.

rows.text: Left hand grip remains weaker than right
rows.rationale: The weakness is unchanged. Keep comparing grips at every check.

rows.text: Left corner of the mouth droops when he smiles
rows.rationale: A new deficit. Report it even though the total score went up.

question.takeaway: Improving is not the same as back to baseline. A rising score can still hide a new deficit.
question.strategy: Judge each row on its own. A better total does not make every finding better.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: GCS 10, withdrawal only, pupil 5 mm and sluggish.
Score, commands and pupil.

steps.action: Catch the unchanged and the new
steps.detail: Weak grip unchanged; facial droop is new.

elimination.verdict: Improved, improved, improved, not improved, not improved.

questions.stem: A daughter says her mother was normal at breakfast at 0700. At 0930 the nurse finds the mother with sudden left arm weakness and calls a stroke alert. Which onset time does the nurse report?

options.text: 0700, when she was last known well
options.rationale: Last known well starts the treatment clock and decides whether a clot buster or clot removal is possible.

options.text: 0930, when the weakness was found
options.rationale: This is the time of discovery. Using it could make an ineligible patient look eligible.

options.text: The time the stroke alert was called
options.rationale: The alert time tracks the team's response, not the stroke.

options.text: The time she arrives at the CT scanner
options.rationale: Arrival time does not reset the clock.

questions.takeaway: Time is brain. Report last known well, not the time symptoms were found.
questions.strategy: The discovery time feels like onset. Ask when she was last seen normal.

steps.detail: Found at 0930, normal at 0700.
Alert and CT times are not onset.

elimination.verdict: 0700, last known well.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old patient has trouble finding words, right-sided weakness, and has been incontinent of urine. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Provide perineal care.
options.rationale: Important for skin, but not the priority.

options.text: Assess the gag reflex.
options.rationale: Any stroke can cause dysphagia. Aspiration threatens the airway.

options.text: Elevate the head of the bed to 30 degrees.
options.rationale: A good supportive action, but it does not assess the threat.

options.text: Change the bed linens.
options.rationale: Comfort and skin care come later.

questions.takeaway: Airway comes first. Check swallowing and gag before anything else; the visible problem is often a distractor.
questions.strategy: Ignore the most visible problem and look for the ABC threat.

steps.detail: Incontinence is visible, but it is not life threatening.
Stroke can cause dysphagia and aspiration.
C is an intervention; B assesses the actual risk.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient admitted yesterday with a stroke asks for breakfast. Which task can the RN delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Perform the bedside swallow screen.
options.rationale: Swallow assessment is an RN responsibility.

options.text: Feed the patient after the RN confirms the swallow screen was passed.
options.rationale: Feeding can be delegated once swallowing is confirmed safe.

options.text: Give the patient sips of water to see how well she swallows.
options.rationale: This is a swallow assessment.

options.text: Feed the patient now because she is hungry.
options.rationale: Feeding before a swallow screen risks aspiration.

questions.takeaway: The RN does the swallow screen. Assistive personnel can feed only after the screen is passed.
questions.strategy: Assessment stays with the RN. Look for the option that keeps it there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A and C are both swallow assessments.
D skips the screen.
B has the RN confirming first.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient is 24 hours after an ischemic stroke with right arm weakness present since admission. Which finding at the 1000 neuro check requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Right arm weakness unchanged from admission
options.rationale: This is the patient's known deficit and has not changed.

options.text: New restlessness and confusion
options.rationale: Declining LOC, including restlessness and confusion, is the earliest sign of increased ICP.

options.text: Blood pressure unchanged from the last check
options.rationale: A stable blood pressure is not a new cue.

options.text: Pupils 3 mm, equal and brisk, as at baseline
options.rationale: Unchanged pupils are reassuring. Pupil changes are a later sign.

questions.takeaway: The earliest sign of increased ICP is a change in LOC. Fixed pupils, posturing and the Cushing triad are late.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with baseline. The only new finding is the one to follow up.

steps.detail: The arm weakness is baseline. The pupils and blood pressure are unchanged.
Restlessness and confusion are new.
A change in LOC is the earliest sign.

elimination.verdict: B requires immediate follow up.

questions.stem: A patient with increased intracranial pressure had BP 128/76, HR 88 and regular breathing at 0800. Which set of findings at 1000 requires immediate follow up?

options.text: BP 132/78, HR 84, breathing regular
options.rationale: These values are close to baseline. Nothing here signals a change.

options.text: BP 172/60, HR 52, breathing irregular
options.rationale: Rising BP with a wide pulse pressure, a falling HR and irregular breathing is the Cushing triad. It is a very late sign of rising ICP.

options.text: BP 124/74, HR 92, breathing regular
options.rationale: A small rise in HR with a stable BP does not match the ICP pattern.

options.text: BP 136/82, HR 80, breathing regular
options.rationale: The BP rose slightly but the pulse pressure is not wide. The HR and breathing are stable.

questions.takeaway: The Cushing triad is hypertension with a widened pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular breathing. It is a very late ICP sign that needs immediate action.
questions.strategy: Look for BP and HR moving in opposite directions. BP up with HR down is the brainstem alarm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A, C and D sit close to the 0800 values.
Only B shows BP up, HR down and a new breathing change.

elimination.verdict: B is the Cushing triad and needs immediate follow up.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with increased ICP who needs a bath, linen change, suctioning, and repositioning. What is the best plan?

options.text: Do all of the care at once so the patient can rest afterward.
options.rationale: Back-to-back care can spike ICP.

options.text: Space the care out with rest periods between activities.
options.rationale: Clustering raises ICP. Spacing care keeps pressure down.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed flat during care.
options.rationale: HOB up per protocol, often 30 degrees, helps venous drainage.

options.text: Suction every hour to keep the airway clear.
options.rationale: Suction only when needed; suctioning raises ICP.

questions.takeaway: With high ICP you space out care. This is the opposite of the usual rule to cluster care.
questions.strategy: Watch for a usually correct rule that flips for this patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clustering is usually right, but not with high ICP.
Flat HOB and routine suctioning raise ICP.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes arrives with slurred speech and confusion. Blood glucose is 52 mg/dL. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Prepare the patient for a fibrinolytic.
options.rationale: Symptoms may be from hypoglycemia, not stroke.

options.text: Treat the hypoglycemia per protocol, then reassess the neurologic status.
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia mimics stroke. Correct it and recheck.

options.text: Complete the NIHSS before treating the glucose.
options.rationale: Delays a quick, reversible fix.

options.text: Give a regular meal tray.
options.rationale: Swallowing is not confirmed, and the glucose needs faster treatment.

questions.takeaway: Low glucose looks exactly like a stroke. Check glucose promptly, treat hypoglycemia first, then reassess.
questions.strategy: Fix the reversible cause before starting treatment for the scary diagnosis.

steps.detail: Glucose of 52 explains the symptoms.
A gives a clot buster before the mimic is ruled out.
D ignores swallow safety.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A husband reports his wife went to bed feeling normal at 2300. She woke at 0630 unable to lift her right arm. Which conclusion about clot buster timing is correct?

options.text: She is within 30 minutes of onset
options.rationale: 0630 is when the deficit was found. The clock starts when she was last normal.

options.text: She is over 7 hours from last known well
options.rationale: Last known well is 2300. That places her past the standard 4.5 hour window, so treatment depends on advanced imaging.
