options.rationale: Correct. Glargine covers 20 to 24 hours or more with no pronounced peak.

options.text: "Lantus works like my NovoLog but lasts longer."
options.rationale: Needs follow up. NovoLog is rapid-acting with a defined peak. They differ in more than duration.

options.text: "Lantus peaks while I sleep, so my sugar drops most then."
options.rationale: Needs follow up. Lantus has no pronounced peak.

questions.takeaway: Lantus is glargine and Levemir is detemir. Both are long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak, lasting 20 to 24 hours or more.
questions.strategy: No pronounced peak is the defining feature. It explains why basal insulin is not timed to meals.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lantus is basal with no pronounced peak.
Basal insulin is not tied to meals.
Both give Lantus a peak it does not have.

elimination.verdict: B shows understanding.

questions.concept: Lantus is glargine and Levemir is detemir. Both are long-acting basal insulin with an onset of 1 to 2 hours, no pronounced peak and a duration of 20 to 24 hours or more. Never mixed with other insulin types.

questions.stem: The nurse observes a student perform a fingerstick glucose on a patient whose hands are cold. Which actions indicate correct technique? Select all that apply.

options.text: Verifies the patient's identity first
options.rationale: The first check for any procedure.

options.text: Washes and dries the patient's hands
options.rationale: Residual water dilutes the sample.

options.text: Holds the finger under hot running water
options.rationale: Hot water risks a burn. Gentle warming is enough.

options.text: Punctures the side of the fingertip
options.rationale: Less painful than the pad and gives a good sample.

options.text: Squeezes the finger firmly for a quick sample
options.rationale: Squeezing dilutes the sample with tissue fluid.

options.text: Lets the hand hang down to improve flow
options.rationale: Lowering the hand helps blood flow without risk.

questions.takeaway: Verify identity, wash and dry, use the side of the fingertip, warm gently or lower the hand. Avoid squeezing.
questions.strategy: Cold hands tempt shortcuts. Reject anything that burns the skin or dilutes the sample.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: C and E trade accuracy or safety for speed.
A, B, D and F are standard technique.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D and F are selected.

questions.concept: Before a fingerstick: verify identity, wash and dry hands, check glucometer function, strip compatibility and expiration. Assess the site. Puncture the side of the fingertip and avoid excessive squeezing, which dilutes the sample.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old has lows only on days he injects insulin into his thigh before a brisk walk. After teaching, which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "I will not inject my thigh right before a walk."
options.rationale: Exercise speeds absorption from the working limb.

options.text: "My thigh absorbs insulin faster than my abdomen."
options.rationale: This is reversed. The abdomen is the fastest site.

options.text: "Every site absorbs the same, so walking is the problem."
options.rationale: Absorption differs by site and by activity.

options.text: "I will rub the site after injecting."
options.rationale: Massage alters absorption and is avoided.

questions.takeaway: Absorption differs by site: abdomen fastest, then arm, thigh, buttock. Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb.
questions.strategy: The lows happen only on walking days. The correct statement links the thigh to the walk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thigh injection plus walking equals faster absorption.
Every site is the same is an absolute.
Reversed order and massage are both wrong.

elimination.verdict: A shows understanding.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin absorption differs by site: abdomen is fastest, then upper arm, then thigh, then buttock or hip. Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb.

questions.stem: A student gives NPH insulin in the abdomen of a client whose glucose readings have been erratic. Which student action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Pinches up the skin and fat before inserting
options.rationale: Correct technique that keeps the dose in the subcutaneous tissue.

options.text: Holds the needle in place briefly before withdrawing
options.rationale: Correct. It keeps the dose from leaking out.

options.text: Withdraws the needle at the angle it went in
options.rationale: Correct. It limits tissue trauma.

options.text: Massages the site after withdrawing the needle
options.rationale: Massage speeds and alters absorption, which can add to erratic glucose readings.

questions.takeaway: Do not massage an insulin site. It changes how fast the dose is absorbed.
questions.strategy: Three options are correct technique. Find the one that could explain this client's erratic readings.

steps.detail: Requires intervention means find the error.
Erratic glucose points to absorption.

elimination.verdict: Massaging the site.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin technique: pinch the skin and subcutaneous fat, insert at a 90 degree angle, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold the needle briefly before withdrawing, withdraw at the same angle. Dispose in a sharps container immediately.

questions.stem: An order reads regular insulin 6 units subcutaneously before breakfast. The tray is expected in 30 minutes. The patient is alert, eating normally, and his fingerstick glucose is 156 mg/dL. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give the dose now
options.rationale: Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so giving it half an hour before the tray matches its action to the food.

options.text: Hold the dose until bedtime
options.rationale: Separates a mealtime insulin from the meal it covers.

options.text: Give the dose when the tray arrives
options.rationale: That timing belongs to rapid-acting insulin.

options.text: Give the dose after he has eaten half the meal
options.rationale: Leaves the insulin peaking after the carbohydrate has been absorbed.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting goes just before or with the meal. Regular goes about 30 minutes before, because its onset is slower. Rapid-acting insulin such as lispro or aspart has an onset of 10 to 30 minutes and is given just before or with meals. Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes and is given about 30 minutes before meals.
questions.strategy: Match the onset to the food. The number to remember is not the duration but when the insulin starts working relative to when carbohydrate arrives.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Regular, which is short-acting.
That timing belongs to rapid-acting insulin.
Leaves the insulin peaking after the carbohydrate has been absorbed.
Separates a mealtime insulin from the meal it covers.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so giving it half an hour before the tray matches its action to the food.

questions.concept: Rapid-acting insulin such as lispro or aspart has an onset of 10 to 30 minutes and is given just before or with meals. Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes and is given about 30 minutes before meals.

questions.stem: A patient is alert and swallowing safely. His fingerstick glucose is 58 mg/dL. His rapid-acting insulin is due now and his breakfast tray has not arrived. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the scheduled insulin
options.rationale: Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient. It would drive the glucose lower.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: A glucose under 70 is treated before anything else, and he is conscious and able to swallow.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The recheck follows treatment rather than replacing it.

options.text: Wait for the breakfast tray
options.rationale: Delays treatment while the glucose continues to fall.

questions.takeaway: Treat first, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then work out why it happened. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient. For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat treatment if still low.
questions.strategy: The scheduled insulin and the missing tray are both deliberate pressure. Neither changes the rule that a glucose under 70 is treated now.

steps.detail: 58, which is under 70.
Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.
The recheck follows treatment rather than replacing it.
Delays treatment while the glucose continues to fall.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: a glucose under 70 is treated before anything else, and he is conscious and able to swallow.

questions.concept: For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat treatment if still low. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.

questions.stem: During her morning insulin round a nurse is told the breakfast trays are delayed by an hour. Two of her patients are due rapid-acting insulin and one is due long-acting basal insulin. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hold the rapid-acting Humalog until the tray is actually in front of the patient
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin begins working in 10 to 30 minutes, so giving it an hour before food creates a low.

options.text: Recheck the blood glucose if there is any further delay
options.rationale: Reduced or delayed intake is a cause of inpatient hypoglycemia.

options.text: Notify the provider if the delay affects the prescribed regimen
options.rationale: The regimen was written around a meal schedule that has changed.

options.text: Give the Humalog now so the round stays on time
options.rationale: Prioritizes the schedule over the patient and produces the exact mismatch that causes hypoglycemia.

options.text: Give the patient's Lantus as scheduled
options.rationale: Long-acting basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not timed to food, so a delayed tray does not change it.

options.text: Give a double dose of Humalog once the tray arrives to make up the delay
options.rationale: Doubling a mealtime dose has no basis and creates a serious hypoglycemia risk.

questions.takeaway: Mealtime insulin waits for the meal. Basal insulin does not, because it is not matched to food. Incorrect insulin type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Mealtime insulin is held until food is present; basal insulin is not timed to food.
questions.strategy: This single scenario separates the two classes. If a delayed tray changes whether you give it, it is a mealtime insulin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Humalog is mealtime; Lantus is basal.
Convenience over the patient.
Doubling has no basis.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.concept: Incorrect insulin type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Mealtime insulin is held until food is present; basal insulin is not timed to food.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed regular insulin 6 units and NPH 14 units in one syringe. The nurse sees a student withdrawing the NPH first. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Let the student continue, since the total dose will be correct
options.rationale: The syringe now holds NPH, so entering the regular vial will contaminate it with NPH and change its action.

options.text: Stop the student, discard the syringe and redraw with regular first
options.rationale: Clear before cloudy keeps NPH out of the regular vial. Starting over is the only way to protect both the vial and this dose.

options.text: Have the student inject the NPH back into its vial
options.rationale: Returning drawn insulin to a vial risks contamination and an inaccurate dose.

options.text: Let the student finish, then roll the syringe to mix
options.rationale: Rolling the syringe does nothing to undo contamination of the regular vial.

questions.takeaway: When mixing, draw regular before NPH. A syringe holding NPH should never enter the regular vial.
questions.strategy: Ask what the next step would do to the regular vial, not only to this dose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH was drawn first.
NPH would contaminate the regular vial.
Discard and redraw clear before cloudy.

elimination.verdict: Stop, discard and redraw with regular first.

questions.concept: When mixing, inject air into the cloudy NPH vial first, then into the clear vial. Draw the clear insulin first, then the cloudy, so the clear vial is never contaminated with suspension.

questions.stem: A patient taking glyburide and metoprolol is confused and sweating before lunch. Her heart rate is 64. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Check her blood glucose now
options.rationale: Metoprolol blunts the tachycardia of a low. Confusion with sweating still points to hypoglycemia.

options.text: Rule out a low because her heart rate is normal
options.rationale: A beta blocker masks the fast heart rate, so a normal rate does not rule out a low.

options.text: Give the next metoprolol dose as ordered
options.rationale: This ignores a possible low.

options.text: Reorient her and recheck in one hour
options.rationale: Waiting delays treatment of a possible low.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia. Sweating usually persists. Shakiness and a fast heart rate may not.
questions.strategy: The normal heart rate is the trap. The beta blocker explains it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glyburide can cause lows. Metoprolol hides the fast heart rate.
A normal rate does not rule out a low.
Neither checks the glucose.

elimination.verdict: A comes first.

questions.stem: A patient who takes acarbose with each meal becomes hypoglycemic. Which does the nurse administer?

options.text: Table sugar dissolved in water
options.rationale: Sucrose has to be split into glucose and fructose first, and acarbose is blocking exactly that step. This is the trap.

options.text: A slice of bread
options.rationale: A complex carbohydrate needing digestion, and slower still.

options.text: A glass of milk
options.rationale: Lactose also requires breakdown, and milk raises glucose too slowly for an acute low.

options.text: Glucose tablets
options.rationale: Acarbose blocks the enzyme that breaks table sugar into absorbable glucose, so sucrose will not work. Glucose tablets need no digestion.

questions.takeaway: On acarbose or miglitol, treat hypoglycemia with glucose specifically. Sucrose and starch will not be absorbed.
questions.strategy: This is the one hypoglycemia scenario where the usual juice-or-sugar answer is wrong. The drug name in the stem is the signal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breakdown of complex sugars in the gut.
Both need the blocked enzyme.
Lactose also needs breakdown.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: glucose tablets.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient who is starting empagliflozin for type 2 diabetes. Which statement by the patient indicates understanding?

options.text: "I will report burning when I urinate or genital itching."
options.rationale: This drug puts glucose into the urine. That raises the risk of urinary and yeast infections.

options.text: "This pill is a form of insulin."
options.rationale: There is no oral insulin.

options.text: "My urine should stay free of sugar now."
options.rationale: Glucose in the urine is how the drug works.

options.text: "I only take it when my sugar is over 200."
options.rationale: It is taken on a schedule.

questions.takeaway: SGLT-2 inhibitors lower glucose by excreting it in the urine. Expect more urination and watch for infection.
questions.strategy: Know the mechanism. Sugar in the urine explains both the side effect and the teaching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose leaves in the urine.
It contradicts the mechanism.
Not insulin and not taken as needed.

elimination.verdict: A shows understanding.

questions.stem: A patient on metformin is scheduled for a computed tomography scan with iodinated contrast. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give half the usual dose
options.rationale: Not a recognized approach. The decision is to hold or not, and it is the provider's.

options.text: Confirm with the provider that the metformin is held around the study
options.rationale: Contrast can impair kidney function, and metformin cleared by the kidneys accumulates. The build-up risks lactic acidosis.

options.text: Give the metformin with a full glass of water before the scan
options.rationale: Water does not protect the kidneys from the contrast or clear the drug faster.

options.text: No action, since metformin does not interact with contrast
options.rationale: It does, and this is one of the most tested medication-procedure interactions.

questions.takeaway: Metformin is held around iodinated contrast because contrast-related kidney impairment lets it accumulate and cause lactic acidosis.
questions.strategy: Ask what clears the drug and what the contrast does to that organ.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: By the kidneys.
Impair kidney function.
A well-known interaction.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: confirm the hold with the provider.

questions.stem: A clinic nurse calls patients who each take one oral diabetes drug alone. Each skipped lunch today. Which patients need follow up for hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 66-year-old taking glipizide
options.rationale: A sulfonylurea forces insulin release. A skipped meal can lead to a low.

options.text: A 71-year-old taking glyburide
options.rationale: Also a sulfonylurea.

options.text: A 59-year-old taking glimepiride
options.rationale: Also a sulfonylurea.

options.text: A 54-year-old taking metformin
options.rationale: Metformin alone rarely causes a low.

options.text: A 62-year-old taking sitagliptin
options.rationale: This works only when glucose is rising.

options.text: A 68-year-old taking acarbose
options.rationale: Acarbose slows carbohydrate absorption. Alone it rarely causes a low.

questions.takeaway: Sulfonylureas cause lows because they force insulin release regardless of glucose. Metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors and acarbose do not.
questions.strategy: The skipped lunch is the cue. Ask which drug keeps pushing insulin without food.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glipizide, glyburide and glimepiride share one mechanism.
They do not force insulin release.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.stem: While preparing a bedtime dose of insulin glargine, the nurse notices the solution in the vial is cloudy. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Discard the vial and obtain a new one
options.rationale: Glargine is a clear solution. Cloudiness means contamination or degradation.

options.text: Roll the vial gently, then draw the dose
options.rationale: Rolling is for NPH. Glargine should never look cloudy.

options.text: Give the dose because it is a suspension
options.rationale: Glargine is not a suspension.

options.text: Draw it with regular insulin to clear it
options.rationale: Long-acting insulin is never mixed.

questions.takeaway: Only NPH and premixes that contain it look cloudy. Glargine is always clear, so a cloudy vial is discarded.
questions.strategy: Match the look to the class. Cloudy only fits N.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glargine is clear.
Both treat glargine like NPH.
Glargine is never mixed.

elimination.verdict: A is correct.

questions.stem: A patient's glucose is 240 mg/dL at 0700. The 0300 check showed 48 mg/dL. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Report the 0300 low along with the morning high
options.rationale: An overnight low that rebounds is the Somogyi pattern. The provider needs both values.

options.text: Request more evening insulin for the high reading
options.rationale: More insulin would deepen the overnight low that caused the rebound.

options.text: Repeat the morning reading as a likely meter error
options.rationale: The overnight trend explains the high. It is not an error.

options.text: Treat it as dawn phenomenon and take no action
options.rationale: Dawn has no preceding low. The 48 separates them.

questions.takeaway: Somogyi: an overnight low rebounds to a morning high. Dawn rises without a low. The 0200 to 0300 check tells them apart.
questions.strategy: Do not treat the morning number alone. The 0300 low explains it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A low at 0300 then a high at 0700 is a rebound.
It treats only the high.
Both ignore the 0300 low.

elimination.verdict: A is correct.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches sick day rules to a patient with type 1 diabetes who has influenza and is vomiting. Which statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I keep taking my insulin even if I cannot eat."
options.rationale: Illness raises glucose. Stopping insulin leads to ketoacidosis.

options.text: "I check my sugar every three to four hours."
options.rationale: Illness makes glucose unpredictable.

options.text: "I test for ketones if my sugar stays over 240."
options.rationale: Ketones signal ketoacidosis may be developing.

options.text: "I take small sips of fluid often."
options.rationale: Vomiting plus high glucose dehydrates quickly.

options.text: "I stop insulin until I am eating again."
options.rationale: The most dangerous sick day error.

options.text: "I wait for the fever to break before calling."
options.rationale: Persistent vomiting or ketones need reporting now.

questions.takeaway: Sick days: never stop insulin, check glucose every three to four hours, test ketones above 240, keep fluids going.
questions.strategy: Illness raises insulin need. Any statement that cuts insulin or delays a call is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Keep insulin versus stop insulin. Keep wins.
Waiting delays care.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D are selected.

questions.stem: A patient using an insulin pump reports the glucose has risen from 140 to 310 mg/dL over four hours and ketones are now present. Which does the nurse suspect first?

options.text: A faulty glucose meter
options.rationale: The ketones corroborate the reading. Two findings agreeing is not a meter fault.

options.text: The pump is delivering too much basal insulin
options.rationale: Too much would lower the glucose, not raise it, and would not produce ketones.

options.text: An expected rise after a high-carbohydrate meal
options.rationale: A meal does not produce ketones, and the rise would not continue over four hours.

options.text: An interruption in insulin delivery at the site or in the tubing
options.rationale: A pump delivers only rapid-acting insulin, with no long-acting reserve. An occlusion or dislodged cannula leaves the patient with no insulin at all within hours.

questions.takeaway: Pump patients have no long-acting insulin on board. An interruption produces hyperglycemia and ketones within hours.
questions.strategy: Ask what a pump does and does not deliver. The ketones are the finding that rules out a simple meal-related rise.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid-acting only, no basal reserve.
They indicate no insulin is reaching the patient.

steps.action: Cut the meal and meter options
steps.detail: Neither explains ketones.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: an interruption in delivery.

questions.stem: A student is about to puncture a 68-year-old's finger for a 0730 glucose check. The meter passed its control check, but the strip vial expired last month. Which action should she take next?

options.text: Proceed, since the meter passed its control check
options.rationale: The control check tests the meter, not these strips.

options.text: Get an in-date vial of compatible strips before the puncture
options.rationale: Expired strips give unreliable results. Replacing them before the puncture spares the client a second stick.

options.text: Use the strips because the vial was sealed
options.rationale: Expiration applies whether or not the vial was opened.

options.text: Run the test and repeat with a new strip only if abnormal
options.rationale: An expired strip can give a falsely normal value that is never rechecked.

questions.takeaway: Check strip dates before you puncture. A passing meter check does not validate expired strips.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option finds a reason to use the strips anyway.

steps.detail: Three options use the expired strips anyway.
Replace before puncturing.

elimination.verdict: Get in-date strips first.

questions.concept: Before a fingerstick: verify identity, wash and dry hands, check glucometer function, strip compatibility and expiration, and assess the site. Puncture the side of the fingertip and avoid excessive squeezing, which dilutes the sample.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old admitted for cellulitis has fingerstick glucose readings of 148, 171 and now 194 mg/dL. He is alert, eating half of each meal and has no shakiness. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Document the value as within target
options.rationale: 194 is above the usual inpatient target, and the trend is rising.

options.text: Assess him and review the orders for glucose parameters
options.rationale: A rising trend during infection needs assessment and a check of the correction or notify parameters.

options.text: Give an extra dose of mealtime insulin
options.rationale: Insulin needs an order. The nurse does not add doses.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: That treats a low. His glucose is high.

questions.takeaway: A rising glucose trend during infection calls for assessment and a check of the orders, not unprescribed treatment.
questions.strategy: Look at the trend, not one number, and stay inside scope.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rising all day.
Carbohydrate treats lows.
No extra insulin without an order.

elimination.verdict: Assess and review the orders.

questions.concept: Under 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia and an immediate safety concern. 70 to 180 mg/dL is the common inpatient target range. Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia requiring assessment and review of orders.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old on insulin had a glucose of 61 mg/dL at 0600 and received 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate. At 0615 it is 66 mg/dL and he feels less shaky. Breakfast arrives at 0730. Which action does the nurse take now?

options.text: Give another 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: He is still below 70. The rule of 15 says treat again and recheck in 15 minutes.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before treating
options.rationale: He is still low now. Rechecking without treating wastes time.

options.text: Document the improvement and wait for breakfast
options.rationale: Feeling better is not the target. 66 is still hypoglycemia, and breakfast is over an hour away.

options.text: Give his mealtime insulin early
options.rationale: Insulin would drive a low glucose lower.

questions.takeaway: Treat until the glucose is at least 70. Feeling better does not end the rule of 15.
questions.strategy: The improvement is the trap. Judge by the number.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 66 is below 70.
Another 15 to 20 g, recheck in 15 minutes.

elimination.verdict: Treat again.

questions.concept: For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat treatment if still low. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old has Humalog 6 units ordered with meals and Lantus 18 units daily, neither given yet. After two bites of breakfast he says he is nauseated and pushes the tray away. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Give the Humalog now since the tray was delivered
options.rationale: Rapid acting insulin with almost no food risks a low within the hour.

options.text: Give half the Humalog to match his intake
options.rationale: The nurse cannot change a dose without an order.

options.text: Hold the Humalog and notify the provider about his intake
options.rationale: Mealtime insulin is matched to food. With almost no intake, hold it and report.

options.text: Hold both the Humalog and the Lantus
options.rationale: Lantus is basal insulin that covers needs between meals. Holding it risks hyperglycemia.

questions.takeaway: Rapid acting insulin follows food. Basal insulin does not. Hold the mealtime dose and report, but do not hold basal insulin without an order.
questions.strategy: Separate the two insulins. Only one is tied to the meal he did not eat.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Humalog is mealtime. Lantus is basal.
Almost no food, so hold Humalog.
No dose changes without an order.

elimination.verdict: Hold Humalog and notify.

questions.concept: Incorrect insulin type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Mealtime insulin is held until food is present; basal insulin is not timed to food.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed regular insulin 5 units and NPH 12 units in one syringe. The student drew regular to the 5 unit mark, then NPH to the 19 unit mark. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose, since 2 extra units is a small difference
options.rationale: Any dose error with a high alert drug is an error. Two extra units of NPH can cause a low hours later.

options.text: Return 2 units to the NPH vial
options.rationale: The syringe holds both insulins, so returning any would put regular into the NPH vial.

options.text: Expel 2 units into the sink and give the rest
options.rationale: The extra is mixed with regular, so expelling it removes some of each and leaves both doses wrong.

options.text: Discard the syringe and redraw, with the NPH to the 17 unit mark
options.rationale: Once mixed, an overdraw cannot be corrected. Redraw so the total is 5 plus 12, or 17 units.

questions.takeaway: The second insulin is drawn to the total of both doses. An overdraw in a mixed syringe means discard and start again.
questions.strategy: Add the doses first. Then ask whether any fix can separate insulins that are already mixed.

steps.detail: 5 plus 12 is 17, not 19.
Returning or expelling removes a mix of both insulins.
Discard and redraw.

elimination.verdict: Discard and redraw to the 17 unit mark.

questions.concept: When mixing, inject air into the cloudy NPH vial first, then into the clear vial. Draw the clear insulin first, then the cloudy, so the clear vial is never contaminated with suspension. Long-acting insulins are never mixed.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old receiving NPH in the abdomen twice daily has a small bruise at yesterday's left lower abdominal site. The rest of the abdomen is intact. Which site does the nurse choose for today's dose?

options.text: The center of the bruise
options.rationale: Bruised tissue absorbs unpredictably and is painful.

options.text: The left lower abdomen at the edge of the bruise
options.rationale: Too close to injured tissue.

options.text: An intact spot on the abdomen away from the bruise
options.rationale: Rotating within the same region keeps absorption consistent and avoids injured tissue.

options.text: The thigh, to rest the abdomen
options.rationale: Switching regions changes absorption. The rest of the abdomen is intact, so there is no need.

questions.takeaway: Rotate sites within one region to keep absorption steady, and avoid bruised or damaged tissue.
questions.strategy: The intact abdomen is the cue that you do not need to leave the region.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Not in or at the edge of the bruise.
Stay in the abdomen.

elimination.verdict: Intact abdomen, away from the bruise.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin absorption differs by site: abdomen is fastest, then upper arm, then thigh, then buttock or hip. One anatomical site is selected and rotation occurs within that region. Avoid bruised, scarred, inflamed, or damaged areas.

questions.stem: At 1030 a 68-year-old on insulin has a glucose of 52 mg/dL. He is alert, diaphoretic and able to swallow. The nurse gives 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate. Which finding shows the treatment worked?

options.text: At 1045 his glucose is 84 mg/dL
options.rationale: The 15 minute recheck is back above 70. That number shows the low has resolved.

options.text: At 1045 he feels less shaky with a glucose of 66 mg/dL
options.rationale: He feels better, but 66 is still under 70. The treatment is repeated.

options.text: At 1040 his skin is dry and he feels calmer
options.rationale: Fewer adrenergic signs are encouraging. Without a recheck value the glucose recovery is unknown.

options.text: He finished all 15 g within five minutes
options.rationale: This shows the treatment was taken. It does not show what the treatment did.

questions.takeaway: Treat, recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still under 70. The recheck number decides whether the low is resolved. How he feels does not.
questions.strategy: An evaluate question asks for evidence of the outcome. For hypoglycemia that is a recheck of 70 or above at 15 minutes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A glucose of 70 or above on the 15 minute recheck.
66 is still under 70.
Symptoms improved, but there is no recheck value.
This describes the intervention, not the result.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: a recheck of 84 at 15 minutes shows the low has resolved.

questions.concept: For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes and repeat treatment if still low. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old taught to inject NPH insulin yesterday gives his 0800 dose into his abdomen as a return demonstration. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Rolls the vial, pinches the skin, inserts at 90 degrees without aspirating
options.rationale: Every step matches the taught technique. NPH is rolled and subcutaneous insulin is not aspirated.

options.text: Shakes the cloudy vial until it looks evenly mixed
options.rationale: Needs follow up. Shaking froths the suspension and makes an accurate dose hard to draw.

options.text: Pulls back on the plunger to check for blood
options.rationale: Needs follow up. Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin.

options.text: Withdraws the needle as soon as the plunger reaches the bottom
options.rationale: Needs follow up. The needle is held briefly so the full dose is delivered.

questions.takeaway: Roll the cloudy vial, pinch, insert at 90 degrees, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold briefly and withdraw at the same angle.
questions.strategy: In a return demonstration the correct answer has no error in it. Read every step in each option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A demonstration that matches every taught step.
NPH is rolled, not shaken.
Subcutaneous insulin is not aspirated.
The needle is held briefly before it is withdrawn.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: rolling, pinching, a 90 degree angle and no aspiration show the technique was learned.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin technique: pinch the skin and subcutaneous fat, insert at a 90 degree angle, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold the needle briefly before withdrawing, withdraw at the same angle and dispose in a sharps container immediately.

questions.stem: Before lunch, a new nurse on a medical unit checks fingerstick glucose on four patients and states a plan for each. Which plan indicates understanding?

options.text: "Mr. A is 160 mg/dL and eating. I document it and continue his plan of care."
options.rationale: Correct. 70 to 180 mg/dL is the common inpatient target range.

options.text: "Ms. B is 66 mg/dL with no symptoms. I recheck when her tray arrives."
options.rationale: Needs follow up. Under 70 is hypoglycemia and is treated now.

options.text: "Mr. C is 190 mg/dL. I give him 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate."
options.rationale: Needs follow up. Above 180 is hyperglycemia. Carbohydrate would raise it further.

options.text: "Ms. D is 62 mg/dL and feels fine. I treat her only if symptoms develop."
options.rationale: Needs follow up. Under 70 is an immediate safety concern whether or not symptoms are present.

questions.takeaway: Under 70 is treated now. 70 to 180 is the inpatient target. Above 180 calls for assessment and a review of orders.
questions.strategy: Place each number in its range, then check whether the planned action fits that range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 66 and 62 are low. 190 is high. 160 is in range.
Waiting and ignoring a low are unsafe. Carbohydrate for a high is backward.
160 in range is documented.

elimination.verdict: 160 is in the target range.

questions.stem: At 1000 the nurse checks a 64-year-old who received Humulin R 10 units at 0730. His breakfast tray was delayed and has just arrived. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Cool, clammy skin with new irritability
options.rationale: These are signs of hypoglycemia. Regular insulin is peaking now. His meal came late.

options.text: Fingerstick glucose of 150 mg/dL before the dose
options.rationale: This is within the target range of 70 to 180. The pre-dose value is not the problem.

options.text: Humulin R vial that appears clear
options.rationale: Regular insulin is clear. This is expected.

options.text: Dose given in the abdomen
options.rationale: The abdomen is an accepted site and absorbs fastest.

questions.takeaway: Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose. A delayed meal at the peak sets up a low.
questions.strategy: Place 1000 on the regular insulin timeline. Then look for the finding that fits a low.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 1000 is inside the 2 to 4 hour peak.
Clear regular insulin, abdominal site and a pre-dose 150 are all fine.
Cool clammy skin with irritability fits hypoglycemia.

elimination.verdict: Cool, clammy skin with new irritability.

questions.stem: At 1000 the nurse reviews four patients who received insulin this morning. Which patient does the nurse assess first for hypoglycemia?

options.text: Humulin R at 0730, ate 25% of breakfast
options.rationale: Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose, which is 0930 to 1130. Reduced intake at the peak is a key cause of inpatient lows.

options.text: Humulin N at 0800, ate all of breakfast
options.rationale: NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose. The risk starts around noon.

options.text: Lantus at 2100 last night, ate all of breakfast
options.rationale: Lantus is basal insulin with no pronounced peak.

options.text: NovoLog at 0800 with breakfast, ate all of it
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin peaks 30 to 90 minutes after the dose. That window has passed and the meal was eaten.

questions.takeaway: The highest risk is at the insulin's peak. Reduced intake at the peak makes it higher still.
questions.strategy: For each patient, work out where the insulin is in its action at 1000. Then check whether food matched it.

steps.detail: Regular is peaking now. NPH has not peaked. NovoLog has passed its peak. Lantus has none.
Only the regular insulin patient ate little.
Peak plus poor intake.

elimination.verdict: Humulin R at 0730 with 25% of breakfast eaten.

caseStudies.title: Hypoglycemia before lunch on mealtime insulin
caseStudies.intro: A 70 year old woman with type 2 diabetes was admitted 2 days ago for cellulitis of the left leg. She receives regular insulin before meals and basal insulin once a day.

entries.text: Fingerstick glucose checked. Humulin R 8 units given subcutaneously in the abdomen. Breakfast tray due at 0800.
Ate 20% of breakfast. Reports nausea.
Lantus 20 units given subcutaneously.
Call light on. Irritable and tells the nurse to leave her alone. Skin cool and clammy. Hands shaking. States she feels hungry.
T 37.4 C; HR 82; RR 16; BP 132/78; SpO2 97% on room air
T 37.2 C; HR 108; RR 18; BP 134/80; SpO2 97% on room air
Fingerstick glucose 124 mg/dL (70 to 180)
Type 2 diabetes. Cellulitis of the left leg treated with IV antibiotics.
Humulin R 8 units subcutaneously before meals at 0730, 1130 and 1630.
Lantus 20 units subcutaneously daily at 0900.
Hypoglycemia protocol: glucose under 70 and able to swallow, give 15 to 20 g fast acting carbohydrate. Recheck in 15 minutes. Repeat if still under 70. Notify provider.

question.nursesNote: 1100: Call light on. Client is irritable and tells the nurse to leave her alone. Skin cool and clammy. Hands shaking. States she feels hungry. Ate 20% of breakfast because of nausea. Humulin R 8 units given at 0730. HR 108; RR 18; BP 134/80. Left leg dressing dry and intact. Alert and oriented x4.
question.stem: Which findings require follow up? Highlight the findings.

segments.text: irritable and tells the nurse to leave her alone
segments.rationale: Irritability is a hypoglycemia sign. It is often mistaken for a behavioral issue.

segments.text: Skin cool and clammy
segments.rationale: The adrenergic response to a falling glucose. High glucose gives warm dry skin instead.

segments.text: Hands shaking
segments.rationale: Shakiness is usually the earliest warning of a low.

segments.text: States she feels hungry
segments.rationale: Hunger is one of the classic signs of hypoglycemia.

segments.text: Ate 20% of breakfast because of nausea
segments.rationale: Reduced intake is a key cause of inpatient hypoglycemia.

segments.text: Humulin R 8 units given at 0730
segments.rationale: Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose. For a 0730 dose that window is 0930 to 1130.

segments.text: HR 108
segments.rationale: Tachycardia is part of the same adrenergic response.

segments.text: RR 18
segments.rationale: Within the normal range.

segments.text: Left leg dressing dry and intact
segments.rationale: Expected for her cellulitis care.

segments.text: Alert and oriented x4
segments.rationale: Normal. Because she is awake and oriented, treating by mouth is an option if her glucose is low.

question.takeaway: Shaky, sweaty, tachycardic, hungry, irritable. Add a full insulin dose at its peak with a small breakfast and you have a likely low.
question.strategy: The irritability is the trap. It reads like a mood. In a client on insulin it is a cue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cool clammy skin, shaking, a fast heart rate and hunger.

steps.action: Connect the insulin and the meal
steps.detail: Regular insulin at 0730 peaks by 1130. She ate 20% of breakfast.
RR 18, a dry dressing and full orientation.

elimination.verdict: Irritability, clammy skin, shaking, hunger, low intake, the 0730 dose and HR 108.

question.scenario: Before checking the glucose, the nurse reviews which findings separate a low glucose from a high glucose.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is consistent with hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia.

rows.text: Shakiness and diaphoresis
rows.rationale: Sympathetic signs. Usually the earliest warning of a low.

rows.text: Cool, clammy skin
rows.rationale: The adrenergic response makes skin cool and damp.

rows.text: Irritability or anxiety
rows.rationale: The brain is short of glucose. Often mistaken for behavior.

rows.text: Warm, dry, flushed skin
rows.rationale: The skin picture of high glucose.

rows.text: Polyuria developing over the past two days
rows.rationale: Sugar in the urine drags water out with it. It builds over days.

rows.text: Symptoms that come on over minutes to hours
rows.rationale: Hypoglycemia comes on fast. Hyperglycemia builds over days.

question.takeaway: Low glucose is fast, cool, clammy and shaky. High glucose is slow, warm, dry and thirsty with a lot of urine.
question.strategy: Ask how fast it came on and what the skin feels like. Those two questions sort almost every row.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cool and clammy is low. Warm and dry is high.
Minutes to hours is low. Days is high.
Irritability belongs to the low.

elimination.verdict: Hypo, hypo, hypo, hyper, hyper, hypo.

question.stem: Which problem is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Anxiety about being in the hospital
options.rationale: Irritability here is a sign of a low glucose. Calling it anxiety delays treatment.

options.text: Hypoglycemia from mealtime insulin with reduced intake
options.rationale: A full dose of regular insulin at its peak after she ate 20% of breakfast. Her signs fit a low.

options.text: Hyperglycemia from the stress of infection
options.rationale: Illness can raise glucose. Her cool clammy skin and fast onset point the other way.

options.text: Nausea related to her infection
options.rationale: Real and uncomfortable. It matters because it cut her intake. The low is the danger.

question.takeaway: Incorrect type, dose, timing and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Suspect it whenever a client on insulin ate less than planned.
question.strategy: Two options explain the behavior without the glucose. Pick the one that explains every cue in the chart.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Irritability in a client on insulin is a cue, not a personality.
Cool clammy skin and a fast onset do not fit a high.
Nausea caused the problem. The low is the problem.

elimination.verdict: Hypoglycemia from mealtime insulin with reduced intake.

question.scenario: The nurse plans care before checking the client's glucose.
question.stem: For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.

rows.text: Verify the client with two identifiers before the fingerstick
rows.rationale: The first check, as with any procedure.

rows.text: Confirm the strips are in date and compatible with the meter
rows.rationale: A working meter cannot rescue an expired strip. Treatment rides on the number.

rows.text: Lower her cool hand below heart level
rows.rationale: Helps blood pool in a cool finger.

rows.text: Squeeze the finger firmly to get the sample quickly
rows.rationale: Hard squeezing dilutes the sample with tissue fluid.

rows.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast acting carbohydrate if the glucose is under 70
rows.rationale: She is awake and can swallow, so oral treatment is the right first step.

rows.text: Give the 1130 Humulin R on time so it covers lunch
rows.rationale: Insulin is never given to a client who may be hypoglycemic. It would drive the glucose lower.

question.takeaway: Get an accurate number, then treat by the number. Identify, check the strips, use a lowered hand, never squeeze hard. Under 70 means 15 to 20 g of fast acting carbohydrate.
question.strategy: The insulin row sounds efficient because lunch is coming. A mealtime dose is never the answer while a low is suspected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Protect the accuracy of the number
steps.detail: Identity, in date strips, a lowered hand. No hard squeezing.
15 to 20 g of fast acting carbohydrate if she is under 70.
No insulin on top of a suspected low.

elimination.verdict: Indicated, indicated, indicated, not indicated, indicated, not indicated.

entries.text: Fingerstick glucose 58 mg/dL (70 to 180). Awake and able to swallow. 15 g fast acting carbohydrate given by mouth per protocol.
Recheck glucose 64 mg/dL (70 to 180). States she feels less shaky. Skin still damp. Lunch tray due at 1200. Humulin R 8 units due at 1130.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give another 15 to 20 g of fast acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: She is still under 70, so treatment is repeated.

options.text: Recheck the glucose 15 minutes after the second treatment
options.rationale: The recheck tells you whether the treatment worked.

options.text: Hold the Humulin R due at 1130
options.rationale: Insulin is never given to a hypoglycemic client.

options.text: Notify the provider of the low and the reduced intake
options.rationale: The regimen was written for a client who eats. The provider adjusts the plan.

options.text: Document the improvement since she feels less shaky
options.rationale: Feeling better does not mean the glucose has recovered. 64 is still low.

options.text: Recheck in 15 minutes before giving more carbohydrate
options.rationale: The recheck already happened and showed a low. Waiting lets it fall further.

options.text: Give the Humulin R at 1130 so it covers lunch
options.rationale: Adds insulin on top of a low.

options.text: Give half the Humulin R dose to match her smaller intake
options.rationale: Improvises a dose that was never ordered. Dose changes come from the provider.

question.takeaway: Treat, recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still under 70. Hold mealtime insulin while she is low. Tell the provider.
question.strategy: The client's words are the trap. She feels less shaky. The number is 64. The number decides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Read the number, not the feeling
steps.detail: 64 is under 70. Repeat the treatment.
No insulin while she is low. No improvised half dose.
Recheck in 15 minutes. Notify the provider.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

entries.text: Second 15 g of fast acting carbohydrate taken within 5 minutes.
Skin drier. States she feels calmer. Humulin R held. Provider notified.
Recheck glucose 92 mg/dL (70 to 180). HR 86. Alert and oriented x4.
Glucose 96 mg/dL (70 to 180) before lunch. Provider will review the insulin plan.

question.scenario: The nurse evaluates the client's response to treatment.
question.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows the low has resolved.
columns: Does not show the low resolved

rows.text: 1120: glucose 64 mg/dL; feels less shaky
rows.answer: Does not show the low resolved
rows.rationale: She feels better. The value is still under 70.

rows.text: 1122: took all 15 g within 5 minutes
rows.answer: Does not show the low resolved
rows.rationale: Shows the treatment was taken. It does not show what the treatment did.

rows.text: 1130: skin drier; feels calmer
rows.answer: Does not show the low resolved
rows.rationale: Encouraging. Without a recheck value, glucose recovery is unknown.

rows.text: 1137: glucose 92 mg/dL
rows.rationale: The 15 minute recheck is back above 70.

rows.text: 1155: glucose 96 mg/dL before lunch
rows.rationale: Still within the 70 to 180 target. The low has not come back.

answer.r1: Does not show the low resolved
answer.r2: Does not show the low resolved
answer.r3: Does not show the low resolved

question.takeaway: Only a recheck value of 70 or higher shows a low has resolved. How she feels and what she took do not.
question.strategy: Three rows describe real improvement or completed care. Ask of each one: is there a glucose value of 70 or higher?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only rows 4 and 5 give a value.
92 and 96 are above it. 64 is not.
Feeling calmer and finishing the carbohydrate are not outcomes.

elimination.verdict: Does not, does not, does not, shows, shows.
